What is a string in C? Why does a string of n characters need n + 1 bytes? Explain strlen, strcpy, strcat and strcmp with one example each, and write a C program to check whether a word entered by the user is a palindrom Model answer: (b) strlen("Kathmandu") returns 9 (the null is not counted). strcpy(s3, s1) copies s1 into s3, so s3 becomes Kathmandu. strcat(s3, s2) joins s2 onto the end of s3, giving Kathmandu Valley. strcmp(s1, s2) returns 0 when the strings are equal, and here returns -11 because 'K' (65 + 10 = 75) minus 'V' (86) is -11.

Differentiate between a web browser and a search engine with any five points. Model answer: A browser is application software installed on the user's device; a search engine is a website reached through a browser. A browser fetches and renders one page you name; a search engine returns a ranked list of pages matching a query. A browser uses a rendering engine; a search engine uses a crawler, an indexer and a

What is a domain name? What is web hosting? Differentiate between them. Model answer: A domain name is the unique human-readable address of a website, such as neb.gov.np, resolved to an IP address by DNS; it is rented from a registrar and renewed periodically. Web hosting is the service of storing the site's files on a server that is permanently connected to the internet. The domain is the address; the

Differentiate between linear and non-linear multimedia with two examples of each. Model answer: Linear multimedia plays from beginning to end in a fixed order with no user control — examples: a cinema film, an automatically playing slideshow. Non-linear multimedia lets the user choose what to see next through menus, buttons and links — examples: a website, a computer game. Linear content is easier and cheaper to

Differentiate between raster and vector graphics with any five points. Model answer: See the comparison table in §7.2: made of pixels against mathematical shapes; blurs when enlarged against stays sharp; large file size against small; suits photographs against suits logos and maps; JPEG/PNG/GIF/BMP against SVG/AI/EPS/CDR; Photoshop or GIMP against Illustrator or Inkscape.

What is animation? Explain any four types of animation. Model answer: Animation is the illusion of movement created by displaying a rapid sequence of still images that differ slightly, the images being drawn or computed rather than captured. Types: frame-by-frame (cel), where every frame is drawn separately; tweening, where only the key frames are drawn and the software fills in the rest

Explain the audio and video components of multimedia, naming three file formats and one piece of software for each. Model answer: Audio is digitised sound — narration, music and effects — produced by sampling an analogue wave, typically at 44,100 Hz and 16 bits. Formats: MP3 (lossy, small), WAV (uncompressed), MIDI (instructions, not a recording). Software: Audacity. Video is a sequence of frames captured from the real world with synchronised sou

Calculate the uncompressed size, in megabytes, of a 1600 × 1200 image stored in 24-bit colour. Explain why compression is necessary. Model answer: 1600 × 1200 = 1,920,000 pixels. At 24 bits = 3 bytes per pixel, that is 5,760,000 bytes, and 5,760,000 ÷ (1024 × 1024) = 5.49 MB. Compression is necessary because uncompressed images and especially video are far too large to store in quantity or send over a network — one second of uncompressed 1080p video at 30 fps is

Define multimedia and explain the five components with one example of each. Explain any three hardware requirements and any three software requirements of a multimedia computer. Model answer: (b) Hardware: a fast processor to decode compressed video in real time; a graphics card (GPU) to render images and 3D scenes; a sound card with speakers, and large secondary storage because media files are huge; capture devices such as a microphone, scanner, webcam or digital camera. Software: an image editor such as G

Explain any six applications of multimedia, with one sentence on how multimedia helps in each. State any two advantages and any two disadvantages of multimedia. Model answer: (b) Advantages: it uses sight and sound together, so people understand and remember more; the user controls the pace, which suits self-directed learning. Disadvantages: it needs expensive hardware, software and skill to produce; the files are very large, so sharing them needs fast internet and plenty of storage.

Define information security and explain the CIA triad with one example of an attack on each corner. Model answer: Definition as in §8.2. Confidentiality — only authorised people may read the information; attacked by a keylogger capturing a password. Integrity — the information is not altered without permission; attacked by a student changing marks in a result database. Availability — the system is usable whenever a genuine user ne

Differentiate between a virus, a worm and a Trojan horse. State any two symptoms of a malware infection. Model answer: A virus attaches itself to a host file or program and spreads only when that file is copied or executed. A worm is a standalone program that copies itself across a network by itself, needing neither a host nor any user action. A Trojan horse pretends to be a useful program so the user installs it willingly; it does not

What is a digital signature? Explain how it is created and how it is verified. Model answer: Definition as in §8.7. Creation: the sender passes the message through a hash function to get a short message digest, then encrypts that digest with their own private key; the result is the digital signature, which is sent along with the message. Verification: the receiver decrypts the signature with the sender's publi

Define intellectual property right and explain its four types with one example of each. Model answer: Definition as in §8.6. Copyright — the expression of an idea, e.g. source code, a novel or a song; automatic on creation. Patent — a new and non-obvious invention or process, e.g. a new battery chemistry; must be granted. Trademark — a name, logo or slogan identifying a source, e.g. the Nepal Telecom logo. Trade secret

Define cybercrime and explain any six types of cybercrime with one sentence each. State any four measures an ordinary user can take to protect themselves from cybercrime. Model answer: (b) Any four of: use long, unique passwords and enable two-factor authentication; keep the operating system, browser and antivirus updated; never open attachments or click links in unexpected messages, and never share an OTP; check for https and read the domain name before entering anything private; keep regular off-si

concepts.u: Compulsory English: Unit-wise Subjective Question Bank
concepts.t: Why does Aksionov refuse to name Makar Semyonitch to the governor? Model answer: He does not want to bring punishment on another man, and after twenty-six years he has accepted his fate; the refusal shows his calm, humble and forgiving character.

concepts.u: Compulsory English: Unit-wise Subjective Question Bank
concepts.t: What is the central idea of "Corona Says"? Model answer: The central idea is that humans, not the virus, are the greater destroyers of the earth, and that the pandemic has shown human equality and the earth's power to recover.

concepts.u: Compulsory English: Unit-wise Subjective Question Bank
concepts.t: Why do the women in Trifles hide the dead canary? Model answer: They understand that the dead bird proves Mrs Wright's motive, and they sympathise with her loneliness, so they hide it to protect her from the men.

concepts.u: Compulsory English: Model Question Sets and Predicted Questi
concepts.t: What does the title "Trifles" mean in the play? Model answer: "Trifles" means small, unimportant things. The men dismiss the women's interest in kitchen details as trifles, but those details solve the crime.

concepts.u: Compulsory English: Model Question Sets and Predicted Questi
concepts.t: Why is Jean unhappy in "Two Little Soldiers"? Model answer: Jean is jealous and lonely because his friend Luc has started to meet a dairymaid, and he feels left out of the friendship.

concepts.u: Compulsory English: Model Question Sets and Predicted Questi
concepts.t: How does the poet describe the soldier's returned "gifts" in "The Gift in Wartime"? Model answer: The "gifts" are the smell of blood, the soldier's body, medals and loneliness. Calling them gifts is ironic, because each one is a loss.

Why did the Giant build a wall around his garden? Model answer: The Giant came home after seven years and found the village children playing in his garden. He believed that "my own garden is my own garden" and would allow nobody but himself to enjoy it, so he built a high wall and put up a notice-board warning that trespassers would be prosecuted.

Who lived in the garden all the year round after the wall was built, and why were they pleased? Model answer: The Snow and the Frost stayed all year, and they invited the North Wind and then the Hail. They were pleased because Spring had forgotten the garden, which left them free to live there permanently and spoil it — the Snow covering the grass, the Frost silvering the trees, the Hail breaking the roof slates.

What made the Giant realise how selfish he had been? Model answer: One morning he heard a linnet singing and looked out to see the children sitting in the blossoming trees, having crept in through a hole in the wall. In one corner a tiny boy was crying because he could not reach the branches. That sight made the Giant's heart melt and he said, "How selfish I have been!"

Why did the little boy not run away when the Giant came into the garden? Model answer: He did not run because his eyes were so full of tears that he simply did not see the Giant coming. On the symbolic level, his staying suggests that innocent love does not fear, and it is this one child who remains who becomes the means of the Giant's change and salvation.

What did the Giant mean when he said that winter was "merely the Spring asleep"? Model answer: He meant that winter is not death but a pause: the flowers are only resting under the ground and will come back. It shows how much he has changed — the man who once complained that Spring was late can now wait patiently, because he has learned that love, like spring, returns.

What were the wounds on the little boy's hands and feet, and how did he explain them? Model answer: There were the prints of two nails on his palms and two on his little feet — the marks of the Crucifixion. When the Giant angrily demanded who had dared to wound him, the child answered, "Nay! but these are the wounds of Love," identifying himself as Christ, who was wounded out of love for humankind.

How does Wilde use the garden and the seasons to show the inner condition of the Giant? Model answer: Wilde makes the garden a picture of the Giant's inner life, so that the reader can see his moral state. While the children are welcome, all four seasons work: blossom in spring, fruit in autumn, birds in the trees. The moment he builds the wall, the garden is cut off from the ordinary year and locked into a single seas

How did the narrator come to notice the oval portrait? Model answer: At midnight the narrator was displeased with the position of the tall candelabrum and reached out to move it so that its light fell better on his book. The candles then lit a niche that had been hidden in shadow by a bed-post, and the portrait appeared in vivid light.

What exactly was it about the portrait that terrified the narrator? Model answer: It was not the skill of the painting nor the beauty of the face, and he did not mistake it for a living woman. What appalled him was its "absolute life-likeliness of expression" — the picture seemed to be alive, and that impression first startled, then confused and finally overcame him.

Why did the painter's wife hate Art? Model answer: She hated Art because it was her rival. The painter already had a bride in his Art, and the palette and brushes took him away from her, so that she was deprived of her husband's company and even of his face. When he wished to paint her, she therefore heard it as terrible news.

What does the narrator mean by his "incipient delirium", and why does Poe mention it? Model answer: "Incipient delirium" means a fever-madness that is just beginning. Poe mentions it so that the reader cannot be certain whether the portrait is truly uncanny or whether the narrator's sick imagination is at work. This uncertainty deepens the fear and makes the narrator unreliable.

Explain the irony in the painter's words, "This is indeed Life itself!" Model answer: The painter believes he has captured life on canvas, and in that instant he has — but the life came out of his wife. He shouts his triumph over a woman who has just died, and the picture is "Life itself" only because she is no longer alive. Success and disaster arrive in the same moment.

Discuss "The Oval Portrait" as a story about the conflict between art and life. Model answer: Poe builds the story on a single idea: that a work of art may be paid for with a human life, and he presents it literally rather than as a figure of speech. The painter already has "a bride in his Art" before he marries; the living wife is therefore a second wife from the beginning, and she knows it, for she hates only

concepts.u: God Sees the Truth but Waits
concepts.t: What dream did Aksionov's wife have, and how did he react to it? Model answer: She dreamt that he returned from the town and that when he took off his cap his hair had turned completely grey, and she begged him not to start that day. Aksionov laughed at her fear, joked that she was afraid he would go on a spree at the fair, called the dream a lucky sign and drove away.

concepts.u: God Sees the Truth but Waits
concepts.t: What evidence convinced the police-officer that Aksionov was the murderer? Model answer: The police-officer found a blood-stained knife in Aksionov's bag. Added to this were the facts that Aksionov had slept in the room next to the murdered merchant, that the house was locked from inside, and that he had left the inn before dawn. His pale face and broken voice were taken as further proof.

concepts.u: God Sees the Truth but Waits
concepts.t: Why did Aksionov stop sending petitions to the Czar? Model answer: Because his own wife asked him whether he had really committed the murder. Once the person closest to him doubted him, he decided that only God could know the truth and that it was to God alone he should appeal. He gave up all hope of help from men and simply prayed.

concepts.u: God Sees the Truth but Waits
concepts.t: How did Makar Semyonich betray, without meaning to, that he knew about the murder? Model answer: He laughed at the idea that anyone could have hidden a knife in the bag under a sleeping man's head without waking him — a detail only the murderer could know. He also exclaimed how wonderful it was that they should meet, and asked how Aksionov had grown so old, but refused to explain his surprise.

concepts.u: God Sees the Truth but Waits
concepts.t: Why did Aksionov refuse to tell the Governor who had dug the tunnel? Model answer: Telling the truth would have had Makar flogged almost to death, and Aksionov would not take that revenge. He replied that it was not God's will that he should tell, and that the Governor could do as he liked with him. He had also decided, after Makar's threat, to leave the matter "as God shall direct".

concepts.u: God Sees the Truth but Waits
concepts.t: What happened to Aksionov after Makar confessed to the authorities? Model answer: Nothing that could help him. Makar confessed his guilt in spite of Aksionov's words, but by the time the official order for Aksionov's release arrived, Aksionov was already dead. His innocence was proved only after his death.

concepts.u: God Sees the Truth but Waits
concepts.t: Discuss the theme of forgiveness in "God Sees the Truth, but Waits". Model answer: Forgiveness in this story is not a polite word but a costly act, and Tolstoy builds the whole plot so that we can measure its cost. Aksionov has lost twenty-six years, his business, his wife and his children to a crime he did not commit, and he knows exactly who is responsible. When the escape tunnel is discovered, he

concepts.u: God Sees the Truth but Waits
concepts.t: Justify the title of the story with reference to its events. Model answer: The title is a Russian proverb, and the story is arranged to prove both halves of it. "God sees the truth": from the first night, the truth about the murder exists and is known — by Makar Semyonich, and, in the story's religious sense, by God. No human being sees it. The police-officer is honest and completely wrong; t

What is the boy doing at the beginning of the story, and what does it show about him? Model answer: He is sitting alone at the foot of the stairs, carefully picking the scab off his knee and examining the clean pink skin underneath. It shows that he is solitary, patient and closely interested in small, slightly unpleasant things — exactly the kind of attention he will soon turn on the carpet.

What rules does the boy make for his game on the carpet? Model answer: The black parts of the carpet are poisonous snakes, the red parts are red-hot lumps of coal, and only the yellow parts are safe. If he touches black he will be bitten and die; if he touches red he will be burnt. He must cross the whole carpet stepping on yellow alone.

What prize has the boy promised himself for crossing the carpet successfully? Model answer: He has decided that if he crosses the carpet without a single mistake, he will be given a puppy for his birthday, which falls the very next day. The smallness of this reward, set against the death he has imagined for himself, is one of the story's quiet ironies.

How does Dahl show that the game has stopped being a game for the boy? Model answer: Dahl stops describing what the boy pretends and starts describing what he sees: the snakes appear to stir, raise their heads and watch him, and the red looks genuinely hot. At the same time the boy's body reacts — his breathing quickens and he feels dizzy and frightened — which shows that he now believes in the danger.

Why is the last stretch across the black band impossible for him? Model answer: A wide band of black lies across his route, and the nearest yellow patch on the far side is further away than a normal step. He can only reach it by an enormous stretch, with one foot behind and his weight hanging over the black, which leaves him no way to recover if he wobbles.

Why does Dahl end the story with the mother outside in the sunshine? Model answer: Because the sudden distance is more frightening than any description of what happened. After a whole story spent inside the boy's mind, the reader is pushed outside into warm daylight, where an ordinary mother is looking for a child she cannot find. Dahl explains nothing, and the silence does the work.

How does Roald Dahl build tension in "The Wish"? Discuss the techniques he uses. Model answer: Dahl builds tension out of materials that are completely harmless, which is why the effect is so striking. First he establishes the rules, and makes them absolute: black means snakes and death before teatime, red means burning, yellow alone is safe. Because the reader accepts the rules, every later step can be measured

What are Jonathan Iwegbu's five "inestimable blessings"? Model answer: They are five heads that survived the war: his own, his wife Maria's, and those of three of his four children. The fourth child died. He counts survival itself as wealth, which shows both his gratitude and how much the war destroyed.

Why does Jonathan treat his bicycle as a blessing, and how did he save it? Model answer: The bicycle is the machine that restarts his life: used as a taxi between the camps and the military cemetery, it earns him a hundred and fifteen pounds in two weeks. He saved it during the war by paying two pounds to an officer who wanted to commandeer it, and then burying it in the ground until the fighting was over.

How does the Iwegbu family earn a living after they return to Enugu? Model answer: Everyone works. Jonathan rides his bicycle as a taxi and later opens a bar selling palm-wine in his house; Maria makes and sells akara balls; and the children pick mangoes and sell them to soldiers' wives. His old job at the coal mine no longer exists.

What is the "egg-rasher", and how much is it? Model answer: It is the crowd's pronunciation of "ex-gratia award", a payment of twenty pounds made by the treasury to anyone who handed in the now worthless Biafran currency. Jonathan queues for his and receives it, and it is exactly this money the thieves demand that night.

What happens when Jonathan's family shouts for help during the robbery? Model answer: Nothing happens. They call for neighbours, police and soldiers, and no one answers. The leader of the thieves then shouts for the police himself, in mockery, to prove to Jonathan that there is no help anywhere in the neighbourhood.

How does Jonathan react to the loss of his money the next morning? Model answer: He refuses to be upset. He tells the sympathising neighbours not to trouble themselves, saying that the money came to him from nowhere only a few days before, so that losing it means nothing to him; and he repeats "Nothing puzzles God." He and his family are already back at work.

Why is the story called "Civil Peace"? Discuss the irony of the title. Model answer: The title is ironic from beginning to end. It comes from the thief himself, who tells Jonathan through the locked door that the civil war is finished and that this time it is "Civil Peace" — meaning that nobody need be killed provided the money is handed out. Achebe's point is that for ordinary Nigerians the end of the

Discuss "Civil Peace" as a picture of a society just after a war. Model answer: Achebe's post-war Nigeria is drawn in a handful of exact details, and every one of them tells us something. Physically, the country is broken: houses lie in rubble, and Jonathan's flimsy zinc house survives when stronger ones did not, so that survival looks arbitrary rather than deserved. Economically, it is in collaps

Why do the two soldiers go to the same place every Sunday? Model answer: Because the place at the edge of the wood of Champioux reminds them of Brittany. The trees recall the forest of Kermarivan, a large stone recalls the dolmen of Locneuven, and the fields look like Plounivon. Being homesick conscripts, they feel happy nowhere else.

Describe the two soldiers' Sunday meal. Model answer: They buy a piece of sausage, a few cents' worth of bread and a quart of wine in Bezons and carry it wrapped in their handkerchiefs. At their usual corner they take two bricks out of a hedge, light a fire of dry branches and roast the sausage on the points of their knives, then lie on the grass side by side.

How does the dairymaid first show kindness to the soldiers? Model answer: Seeing that they always sit in the same spot, she speaks to them and teases them gently; then, returning with her pail full, she offers them milk, saying it will remind them of home. She has guessed exactly what they are missing, and both soldiers are moved.

What does Luc do during the week that puzzles Jean? Model answer: He obtains leave on a Tuesday and does not come back until ten at night, and then borrows ten sous from a comrade and takes leave again on the Friday. On Sunday he seems strange and disturbed. Jean notices all this, suspects something, but cannot guess that Luc has been meeting the dairymaid.

Why is the sentence "She did not offer him any milk that day" important? Model answer: Because it is the moment Jean's exclusion becomes complete. The milk had been the sign that the girl treated the two friends alike and understood their homesickness; withholding it, with only a careless nod, tells him wordlessly that he is now outside. Maupassant replaces any description of Jean's despair with this one

How does the story end, and what is the last line? Model answer: On the walk home they stop on the bridge at Bezons as they always do. Jean leans further and further over the railing, as if hypnotised by the water, and falls into the Seine; boatmen recover his body the same day. Luc, weeping, reports it at the barracks as an accident, and the story ends with the line "If he had only

Discuss "Two Little Soldiers" as a study of homesickness and friendship. Model answer: Everything the two soldiers value in the story is a substitute for Brittany. They are conscripts from a fishing and farming country, shut up in a barracks at Courbevoie, and their one pleasure is a walk to a wood that resembles the forest of Kermarivan. On the way they stop on the bridge to watch white sails that recal

How does Maupassant prepare the reader for the ending of the story? Model answer: The ending is shocking but not sudden, because almost every element of it has already been planted. The bridge at Bezons is introduced in the third paragraph, and we are told that the soldiers always stop there for several minutes, bending over the railing to watch the Seine. The reader therefore accepts the final paus

What does the astrologer's "professional equipment" consist of, and why does he need it? Model answer: It consists of a dozen cowrie shells, a square piece of cloth covered with mystic charts, a notebook and palmyra writing, together with the sacred ash and vermilion on his forehead and a saffron turban. None of it has any use except display: it makes him look like a holy man with occult knowledge, and so it draws custo

How does the astrologer manage to satisfy his customers without knowing astrology? Model answer: He relies on shrewd guesswork rather than the stars. He lets the customer talk for about ten minutes first, watches him closely, and then gives advice based on what Narayan calls a working analysis of mankind's troubles — marriage, money and the tangles of human ties. Since his answers are flattering and sensible, the

What is the wager between the astrologer and Guru Nayak? Model answer: Guru Nayak challenges him to say something worth hearing. They agree that if the astrologer answers his questions correctly he will be paid a rupee, and that if he is proved wrong he must pay back double. Guru Nayak grips his wrist to hold him to the terms.

Why does the astrologer try to back out of the bargain after the match is struck? Model answer: Because the flame of the match lights the stranger's face, and the astrologer recognises the man he stabbed and threw into a well years before in his own village. He realises he is sitting in front of someone who has come to kill him, and he wants to get away before he is recognised in turn.

What advice does the astrologer give Guru Nayak at the end of the reading, and why? Model answer: He tells him that the man he has been hunting was crushed under a lorry four months ago in a far-off town, and warns him to go home at once and never travel southward again, promising that he will then live to be a hundred. The advice is a lie, and its purpose is to keep Guru Nayak permanently away from the town where

Why does the astrologer say that a great load has gone off him? Model answer: Because he has discovered that Guru Nayak is alive. For years he had believed he had killed a man in his village and had been living with the fear and guilt of it — indeed it was why he ran away, changed his life and became an astrologer. Meeting his victim alive removes that burden at a stroke, and he goes to bed calm

Discuss the irony in "An Astrologer's Day". Model answer: Irony is not one feature of this story; it is the whole design. The largest example is situational. The astrologer is an admitted fraud who, as Narayan tells us on the first page, knows nothing whatever about the stars — and yet the reading he gives Guru Nayak is entirely accurate, down to the knife, the well and the m

How does Narayan prepare the reader for the twist at the end of the story? Model answer: Narayan plays fair with the reader. Every fact needed for the ending is supplied early, but none of it is emphasised. In the opening pages we are told plainly that the astrologer has no knowledge of the stars, which is what makes the later accuracy of his reading significant rather than magical. We are also told, almos

Who is the speaker in "Corona Says", and who is being addressed? Model answer: The speaker is the coronavirus itself, given a human voice by the poet. It addresses the whole human race — the repeated "you" of the poem. The poet himself never speaks directly; his opinion reaches us only through what the virus says.

What charges does the virus bring against human beings? Model answer: The virus accuses human beings of cutting down forests, poisoning rivers and the air, hunting, caging and killing other creatures, and destroying millions of their own kind in wars. Its point is that all this damage was deliberate, long-lasting and far greater than the harm a virus can do.

What changes in nature does the speaker point to as evidence for its argument? Model answer: During the lockdown the air became clear, the rivers ran cleaner, and birds and wild animals reappeared in places from which people had driven them. The earth recovered as soon as human activity stopped, which supports the virus's claim that human beings, not viruses, are the planet's real problem.

Why has the poet chosen free verse instead of a regular metre? Model answer: Free verse has no fixed metre or rhyme, so the poem sounds like ordinary speech rather than a song. That plain, calm, conversational voice makes the virus's accusation sound reasonable, and keeps the reader's attention on the terrible content instead of on pretty sound patterns.

What is a dramatic monologue? Show how "Corona Says" fits the definition. Model answer: A dramatic monologue is a poem in which an invented speaker, who is not the poet, talks at length to a silent listener whose presence we infer from the speech. In "Corona Says" the invented speaker is the virus, the silent listener is humankind, and we learn what humankind feels ("you hate me") only from the virus's wo

Discuss "Corona Says" as a satire on modern human civilisation. Model answer: Satire attacks human folly and wrongdoing by holding it up to ridicule, and that is precisely what this poem does. Its satirical method is to give the speech to the coronavirus, so that human behaviour is described from outside by somebody with no reason to flatter us. The targets are exact. First, our hypocrisy: we ca

The speaker tells human beings that it does not ask whether a body belongs to a rich person or a poor one, to one religion or another, before it enters. Model answer: (a) The speaker is the coronavirus, which the poet has personified and allowed to address humankind throughout the poem. (b) It describes the virus's complete indifference to human distinctions. It infects anyone, and wealth, power, caste, colour, nationality and religion give no protection. This is why the poem presen

What impossible conditions does the speaker use to describe how long he will love? Model answer: He says he will love her till all the seas run dry, till the rocks melt in the sun, and for as long as the sands of his own life keep running. Since none of the first two can happen, the vow means "for ever", measured against the age of the earth and then against his own lifetime.

Why does Burns write in the Scots dialect? Model answer: Scots was the everyday speech of the Ayrshire country people Burns lived and worked among. Using it keeps the poem close to real speech and to oral folk song, gives it a distinct music ("gang", "bonnie", "a'"), and asserts the dignity of ordinary Scottish life at a time when poets were expected to write polished Englis

Who speaks these lines, and in which play and scene do they occur? Model answer: The lines are spoken by Jaques, the melancholy lord, in Shakespeare's comedy As You Like It, Act II, Scene vii. He speaks them in the Forest of Arden, to the banished Duke Senior and his followers, taking up an image the Duke has just used.
List the seven ages of man in the correct order. Model answer: Infant, schoolboy, lover, soldier, justice (judge), pantaloon (the lean slippered old man), and second childishness or oblivion.

What does Shakespeare mean by "the bubble reputation"? Model answer: It is a metaphor for fame won in battle. A bubble is bright and round and attractive, but weightless and certain to burst in a moment. The soldier will face the mouth of a cannon for something that empty, which is Shakespeare's comment on military glory.

How is the schoolboy described, and what does the description suggest? Model answer: He is described with his satchel and "shining morning face", "creeping like snail / Unwillingly to school". The washed, bright face shows he has been carefully prepared by others, while the snail simile shows that he has no wish to go. The gap between the two is the comedy of the second age.

Why is the last age called "second childishness"? Model answer: Because the very old man returns to the condition of the infant he once was. He cannot feed or look after himself, his voice has climbed back to a child's high treble, and finally memory and the senses go. Life is therefore shown as a circle rather than a straight line.

Explain the effect of the repeated word "sans" in the final line. Model answer: "Sans" means "without", and it is repeated four times in one short line. Each repetition removes something more — teeth, eyes, taste, and then "everything". The rhythm of the line therefore imitates the process it describes: loss after loss, until nothing at all is left.

Describe the seven ages of man as Shakespeare presents them, and show how the pictures are chosen to build a single argument. Model answer: Jaques presents seven pictures in time order. The infant is helpless, "Mewling and puking in the nurse's arms". The schoolboy, with satchel and shining morning face, creeps "like snail / Unwillingly to school". The lover sighs "like furnace" and writes a sad ballad to his mistress's eyebrow. The soldier, bearded like t

Discuss "All the World's a Stage" as an extended metaphor. How far do you agree that life is a performance? Model answer: The speech is built on a single comparison carried through to the end, which is what an extended metaphor means. The world becomes a stage, men and women become "merely players", birth and death become "entrances" and "exits", and a lifetime becomes a play in seven acts. Once the metaphor is set, every detail follows f

What is the child doing, and where? Model answer: He is "peering" — looking hard and with concentration — out of a high window, watching the gold of a November sunset. He is alone, still, and completely absorbed in what he sees.

Why does the poet choose a November sunset rather than a summer one? Model answer: November is late autumn in the northern hemisphere, the last month before winter, so the year itself is ending. Putting the day's ending inside the year's ending doubles the idea of things drawing to a close, and prepares us for the poem's real subject, the end of a life.

Why is the pronoun "i" written in lower case? Model answer: To make the self small and humble. A capital "I" would put the speaker at the centre of the poem; the lower-case "i" matches the size of a five-year-old child at a high window and keeps him in proportion to the enormous sunset he is watching. It is one of Cummings's trademark devices, not an error.

What is the effect of putting the last three lines inside brackets? Model answer: The brackets turn the last three lines into a private, inner voice — the child's own feeling, thought rather than spoken. We seem to overhear it instead of being told it, which makes the poem's large statement about death sound gentle and unforced.

Discuss the significance of the sunset in "who are you,little i". Model answer: The sunset is the centre of the poem and its main symbol. On the surface it is simply what the child can see: the gold of the sky at the end of a November afternoon, watched from an upstairs window. But every detail is chosen to make it mean more. It is a sunset, the oldest image in poetry for the close of a life. It i

The child, watching the last gold light of a November evening, feels that if the day has to turn into night, this is a beautiful way for it to happen. Model answer: (a) He is looking through a high window at the gold of a November sunset — the last light of a late-autumn day. (b) The sunset is a symbol for the end of a life, and November, the last month before winter, doubles the idea of things closing. The child's feeling — that if the ending must come, it may come beautifully —

Who is the speaker of "The Gift in Wartime" and whom does she address? Model answer: The speaker is a young Vietnamese widow standing at the grave of the soldier she loved. She addresses him directly as "you", although he is dead and cannot answer. The poem is therefore a one-sided conversation, which is part of its sadness.

What gifts does the speaker offer? Model answer: She offers roses, which she lays on his newly dug grave, and her wedding ring. Beyond these objects she offers herself — her youth, her beauty, her love, and all the years of the life she must now live without him.

What does she receive in return? Model answer: She receives the things war hands out: the smell of blood from his uniform, his dead body returned from the field, the medals and official honours given to the families of the dead, and a lifetime of loneliness and mourning.

Why is the title ironic? Model answer: Because a "gift" is something freely given that the receiver wants, and nothing in the second list is wanted by anybody. Calling blood, a corpse and a medal "gifts" uses the language of love and celebration for the products of killing, and the mismatch is the poem's protest against war.

What do the roses and the wedding ring symbolise? Model answer: The roses stand for love, beauty and mourning, and — because cut flowers die quickly — for how briefly the couple's happiness lasted. The wedding ring is a circle, a symbol of a bond meant to have no end, and it is now being handed over to a grave.

Discuss the use of irony in "The Gift in Wartime". Model answer: Irony means a gap between what is said and what is actually the case, and this poem is built on one enormous example of it. The word "gift" belongs to weddings, birthdays and festivals; it implies choice, affection and pleasure. Tran Mong Tu takes that word and makes it carry the entire traffic of a war. On one side of

The speaker brings roses to lay on a newly dug grave and offers the wedding ring she has worn through her marriage. Model answer: (a) The speaker is a young Vietnamese widow, and she is standing at the freshly made grave of the soldier she loved, during the Vietnam War. (b) The roses stand for love, beauty and mourning; because cut flowers wither within days, they also stand for how short her happiness was. The wedding ring is a circle with no be

How is traditional knowledge passed from one generation to the next? Model answer: It is passed on by the elders, orally and by example — through songs, names, prayers, stories and, above all, through taking part in ceremonies and dances. The learner is present, watches, is given small tasks, and slowly grows into the knowledge instead of being taught it in lessons.

Why does LaPena say that knowledge must be earned? Model answer: Because some knowledge is sacred and powerful, and careless handling can damage both the knowledge and the person. A learner has to show patience, respect and steadiness before more is given; certain songs, names and roles belong to particular families and are not given out generally. Earning it is part of learning to

How does the traditional artist differ from the artist who works for a gallery? Model answer: The traditional artist makes things for use — regalia, baskets, songs, paint for a ceremony — under obligations about how they are made and what may be done with them. A gallery artist makes objects to be looked at, judged and sold. The first kind of art has a job to do in the life of a community; the second is complet

Why is a ceremonial object in a museum not the same object? Model answer: Because its meaning lay in its use. Once it is taken out of the ceremony, put behind glass and labelled, it is cut off from the people, the purpose and the relationships that made it what it was. It looks the same, but it has become information about a tradition rather than a living part of one.

Does LaPena believe a tradition must never change? Explain. Model answer: No. He says that living traditions have always changed — new materials, new songs, new circumstances in every generation — and that a tradition which cannot change has already become a museum piece. What must stay constant is not the outward detail but the relationship behind it: the respect, the purpose and the connec

What does the title "Sharing Tradition" mean in the essay? Model answer: It means passing the tradition on: teaching the right things to the right people at the right time, so that the practice continues into the next generation. It does not mean making everything public. Because each generation holds the tradition in trust rather than owning it, sharing is a duty owed to the ancestors who

State LaPena's central argument in "Sharing Tradition" and show how he builds it. Model answer: LaPena's thesis is that tradition is a living practice rather than a body of information or a collection of objects, that it belongs to a community rather than to an individual, and that anyone who receives it takes on the responsibility of living it properly and handing it on. He builds this in five moves. First he re

How does LaPena describe the relationship between art, ceremony and community? Why does he object to ceremonial objects being collected and displayed? Model answer: In LaPena's account the three are not separable. Ceremony is the centre of community life: dances and songs are not entertainment but work that has to be done, to give thanks, to mark the seasons and the stages of a life, and to keep the relationship between the people and the natural world in good repair. Art exists t

Discuss the style and technique of "Sharing Tradition". How does LaPena persuade a reader who is outside his culture? Model answer: LaPena writes a reflective personal essay in the first person, and his authority is that of a participant rather than a researcher — he has danced, not merely studied. That position governs everything else. The tone is calm, patient and explanatory; he sets out to make an outsider understand rather than to accuse, and

concepts.t: What happened when Steve Jobs turned 30? Model answer: He was fired from Apple, the company he had founded. Apple had grown in ten years into a two-billion-dollar company with over four thousand employees and had just released the Macintosh. The executive Jobs had recruited to run the company with him came to disagree with him about the future, they had a falling out, and

concepts.u: How to Live Before You Die
concepts.t: What does he mean by "don't settle"? Model answer: "Don't settle" means: do not accept second-best work, or a job you merely tolerate, simply because looking for the right one is difficult or slow. Jobs compares the search to a search for love — you will recognise the right thing when you find it — and insists that until you find it you should keep looking rather than

concepts.u: How to Live Before You Die
concepts.t: Explain: "You have to trust in something — your gut, destiny, life, karma, whatever." Model answer: He is admitting that his advice cannot be proved. Since you cannot see ahead, following curiosity instead of a plan requires an act of faith in something — instinct, fate, the divine order, karma. Jobs deliberately offers a list rather than a single name, so that listeners of any religion or none can accept the point.

concepts.u: How to Live Before You Die
concepts.t: Explain: "Your time is limited, so don't waste it living someone else's life." Model answer: He means that the shortness of life makes borrowed living wasteful. Most people spend their days meeting other people's expectations, following inherited opinions, and fearing disapproval — but the time so spent is subtracted from the only life they will ever have. concepts.u: How to Live Before You Die
concepts.t: What does the slogan "Stay Hungry. Stay Foolish." mean? Model answer: They were the farewell words on the back cover of the final issue of The Whole Earth Catalog, and Jobs adopts them as his own wish for the graduates. To "stay hungry" is to remain unsatisfied — to keep wanting to learn and to make, instead of resting on what you have already achieved. To "stay foolish" is to keep the c

concepts.u: How to Live Before You Die
concepts.t: Which style of speech does Jobs use to persuade his audience, and why is his personal-narrative technique so effective? Model answer: Jobs uses the personal narrative or autobiographical style: instead of arguing a thesis, he tells three true stories from his own life and lets each one end in a rule. The speech is informal, conversational and plainly worded, is organised in a tripartite structure announced in advance, and moves steadily from private

How does the writer distinguish between a peaceful age and a heroic age? Model answer: A peaceful age is one in which ordinary safety can be assumed, so that a person may reasonably plan a quiet life; Haldane was born into such an age in 1892 and expected to live in it. A heroic age is one of wars, revolutions and upheavals, in which nothing can be assumed and everyone must improvise. Haldane says that s

Why does the writer want more freedom of speech than most people? Model answer: Because he already has far more freedom than most people and can see exactly where it stops. He would like to say and write in public what he believes about Lord Blank's newspapers, Mr Dash's pills and Sir John Asterisk's beer — all of which, he says, are poisonous — and the law of libel prevents him. He wants freedom

What is the difference between desire and demand according to the writer? Model answer: A requirement or demand is something without which a human life is genuinely damaged: work, freedom, health, friendship. A desire is something that would be pleasant but whose absence can be borne. Haldane illustrates the difference from his own life — he would like a room of his own with books, a motor-car, a daily ba

Why does the writer demand security rather than adventure for others? Model answer: Because he does not trust his own taste for adventure. He admits that peace and security are rightful aims and that his own desire for violent adventure is "probably merely an adaptation to the age in which I live" — a habit forced on him by living through wars, not a virtue. Calling himself "a child of my age, and all

Why can Haldane not be friends with a person whose orders he must obey? Model answer: Because he defines friendship as the society of equals who can criticize one another freely. Where one person must obey another's orders without criticism before or after, criticism in both directions becomes impossible, and so does honesty; what remains is a relation of rank, not friendship. For the same reason he fin

Why does the essayist take his references from ancient philosophers? Model answer: For three reasons. First, they supply ready definitions he does not need to argue for: Aristotle gives him happiness as "unimpeded activity" and Socrates gives him a model of a good death. Second, they give the essay an authority older and wider than any political party, so that his demands look like ordinary human sen

Why does Haldane consider the death of Socrates enviable? Model answer: On three grounds. Socrates died for his convictions when he could easily have saved himself by betraying them; he died at about seventy, still in full possession of his faculties and having completed all the work he could reasonably hope to do; and he died laughing, since his last words were a joke. Discuss the essay in terms of its language, purpose, subject, point of view and mode of writing. Model answer: Subject. The essay's subject is stated in its title: what a human being genuinely requires in order to live well. concepts.u: Word Classes, Contracted Forms and Dictionary Use
concepts.t: The police has arrested the two suspects. Model answer: The police have arrested the two suspects. — police is a plural noun.

concepts.u: Word Classes, Contracted Forms and Dictionary Use
concepts.t: The bus reached at Butwal at seven o'clock. Model answer: The bus reached Butwal at seven o'clock. — reach takes a direct object, arrive takes at/in.

concepts.u: Word Classes, Contracted Forms and Dictionary Use
concepts.t: The dog wagged it's tail when it saw the child. Model answer: The dog wagged its tail … — possessive its has no apostrophe.

concepts.u: Word Classes, Contracted Forms and Dictionary Use
concepts.t: Can you please explain me this rule once more? Model answer: Can you please explain this rule to me once more? — explain cannot take an indirect object without to.

concepts.u: Word Classes, Contracted Forms and Dictionary Use
concepts.t: The students hostel is behind the library. — Insert the apostrophe correctly. Model answer: The students' hostel is behind the library. — plural possessive: apostrophe after the -s.

concepts.u: Word Classes, Contracted Forms and Dictionary Use
concepts.t: The shop is between the bank and the post office. Model answer: Preposition — it relates the noun phrase the bank and the post office to the shop.
The train already left when we arrived at the platform. Model answer: The train had already left when we arrived … — the earlier past action takes the past perfect.
The guests left. Then we cleaned the room. — Join with after, using the past perfect. Model answer: After the guests had left, we cleaned the room. — the earlier action takes had + V3.
The water is essential for all living things. Model answer: Water is essential … — an uncountable noun used generally takes no article.
Why don't we go to Godawari on Saturday? — Rewrite with shall. Model answer: Shall we go to Godawari on Saturday? — shall makes a suggestion with we.
The students of Grade 11 organised a blood donation programme. Model answer: A blood donation programme was organised by the students of Grade 11. — simple past → was/were + V3.
The government has banned single-use plastic in the valley. Model answer: Single-use plastic has been banned in the valley by the government. — present perfect → has been + V3.
The flood had damaged three suspension bridges. Model answer: Three suspension bridges had been damaged by the flood. — past perfect → had been + V3.
Who broke this window? Model answer: By whom was this window broken? — who becomes by whom and moves to the front.
The fields are ploughed by the oxen every Baisakh. Model answer: The oxen plough the fields every Baisakh. — is/are + V3 → simple present.
A new health post is being built by the ward office. Model answer: The ward office is building a new health post. — is being + V3 → present continuous.
The thief had been caught by the neighbours before the police arrived. Model answer: The neighbours had caught the thief before the police arrived. — had been + V3 → past perfect.
The report will have been submitted by the committee by Chaitra. Model answer: The committee will have submitted the report by Chaitra. — will have been + V3 → future perfect.
Let the gate be locked at nine. Model answer: Lock the gate at nine. — Let … be + V3 goes back to an imperative.
A carpenter repaired our main door last week. — Rewrite with had. Model answer: We had our main door repaired last week. — have + thing + V3.
The barber is cutting Bibek's hair at the moment. — Rewrite with is having. Model answer: Bibek is having his hair cut at the moment. — the causative in the present continuous.
The teacher made us to copy the notes again. — Correct the error. Model answer: The teacher made us copy the notes again. — active make takes the bare infinitive.
The road is repairing by the contractor these days. — Correct the error. Model answer: The road is being repaired by the contractor these days. — the passive needs being + V3.
The teacher said, "Water boils at 100 °C." Model answer: The teacher said that water boils at 100 °C. — a universal truth is not backshifted.
The manager said to the clerk, "Bring the file at once." Model answer: The manager ordered the clerk to bring the file at once. — command → to + V1.
The doctor said to the patient, "Don't eat oily food." Model answer: The doctor advised the patient not to eat oily food. — negative command → not to + V1.
The guard ordered us not to park there. Model answer: He said to us, "Don't park here." — not to + V1 becomes a negative imperative; there → here.
The old man asked the boy where he lived. Model answer: The old man said to the boy, "Where do you live?" — the wh- question regains its inversion and do.
The teacher asked us where were we going. Model answer: The teacher asked us where we were going. — a reported question uses statement order.
If I had known your number, I would have called you. — Rewrite without if. Model answer: Had I known your number, I would have called you. — type-3 inversion with had.
If I were the mayor, I would widen this road. — Rewrite without if. Model answer: Were I the mayor, I would widen this road. — type-2 inversion with were.
If it will rain tomorrow, the match will be postponed. Model answer: If it rains tomorrow … — no will in the if-clause of a type 1.
If I would have money, I would buy a new bicycle. Model answer: If I had money … — type 2 takes the simple past in the if-clause.
If she would have called me, I would have gone with her. Model answer: If she had called me … — type 3 takes had + V3, not would have.
If I was you, I would not sign that paper. Model answer: If I were you … — the type-2 subjunctive is were for all persons.
If he had studied harder, he would pass the examination last year. Model answer: … he would have passed the examination last year. — a past result needs would have + V3.
If you will heat ice, it melts. Model answer: If you heat ice, it melts. — a zero conditional uses the present in both clauses.
The farmer is worried. His maize crop failed. Model answer: The farmer whose maize crop failed is worried. — whose shows possession and sits next to farmer.
The tea was too hot for me to drink. — Rewrite using so … that. Model answer: The tea was so hot that I could not drink it. — too … to becomes so … that with a negative result clause.
The boy is my cousin. He won the essay competition. — Join with a relative pronoun. Model answer: The boy who won the essay competition is my cousin. — subject pronoun who, placed next to boy.
The pen was lying on the desk which my uncle gave me. Model answer: The pen which my uncle gave me was lying on the desk. — the clause must stand next to its own noun.

concepts.u: Question Tags, Questions and Subject-Verb Agreement
concepts.t: Where does he live? — Rewrite beginning Do you know … Model answer: Do you know where he lives? — an embedded question keeps statement order and drops does.
The bus reached at Birgunj at midnight. Model answer: The bus reached Birgunj at midnight. — reach takes no preposition.
The soup tastes deliciously. Model answer: The soup tastes delicious. — after a linking verb use an adjective.

Domain of $f$ is $\mathbb{R}-\{3\}$ (denominator zero at 3); range is $\mathbb{R}-\{2\}$ (the value that $f^{-1}$ cannot take).

Find the domain and range of $f(x)=\sqrt{9-x^2}$. Model answer: We need $9-x^2\ge 0$, so $x^2\le 9$ and $-3\le x\le 3$: domain $=[-3,3]$. Inside the root the value runs from $0$ (at $x=\pm3$) to $9$ (at $x=0$), so $f$ runs from $0$ to $3$: range $=[0,3]$.

Define domain, co-domain and range of a function. Find the domain and range of $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x-3}$ and of $g(x) = \sqrt{16 - x^{2}}$. Model answer: The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the co-domain is the set the outputs are declared to lie in; the range is the set of outputs actually attained, always a subset of the co-domain.

Discuss the symmetry of (i) $y^{2} = 8x$, (ii) $x^{2}+y^{2} = 16$, (iii) $y = x^{5}-x$. Derive the formula for the sum of the first $n$ terms of an arithmetic series, and hence find the sum of the first $30$ odd natural numbers. Model answer: Write $S_n = a + (a+d) + \cdots + l$ and again in reverse order; adding the two lines pairs every term to give $a+l$, and there are $n$ pairs, so $2S_n = n(a+l)$ and $S_n = \frac{n}{2}(a+l) = \frac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d]$.

The fourth term of a geometric progression is $24$ and the seventh term is $192$. Find the first term, the common ratio and the sum of the first $10$ terms. Model answer: $ar^{3} = 24$ and $ar^{6} = 192$. Dividing, $r^{3} = 8$, so $r = 2$; then $8a = 24$ gives $a = 3$.

If $a$, $b$, $c$ are in harmonic progression, show that $b = \dfrac{2ac}{a+c}$. Hence find the harmonic mean of $4$ and $12$. Model answer: $a, b, c$ in HP means $\frac1a, \frac1b, \frac1c$ are in AP, so $\frac{2}{b} = \frac1a + \frac1c = \frac{a+c}{ac}$. Cross-multiplying gives $b = \dfrac{2ac}{a+c}$.

The first term of an infinite geometric series is $3$ and its sum is $4$. Find the common ratio and the fourth term. Define the transpose of a matrix. For $A$ with rows $(1,2)$, $(3,4)$ and $B$ with rows $(2,0)$, $(1,3)$, verify that $(AB)^{T} = B^{T}A^{T}$. Model answer: The transpose $A^{T}$ is obtained by interchanging rows and columns, so $(A^{T})_{ij} = a_{ji}$.

If two forces acting at a point are represented in magnitude and direction by the two adjacent sides of a parallelogram drawn from that point, their resultant is represented by the diagonal of the parallelogram through that point.

Show that a particle sliding freely on a smooth plane of inclination $\theta$ has acceleration $g\sin\theta$ down the plane and that the normal reaction is $mg\cos\theta$. The particle of mass $m$ has only two forces on it: the weight $mg$ vertically down and the normal reaction $N$ perpendicular to the plane (the plane is smooth, so there is no friction). Resolve the weight along and perpendicular to the plane: the components are $mg\sin\theta$ down the slope and $mg\cos\the

Solve $|2x-3|\le 5$ and write the solution as an interval. Model answer: $|2x-3|\le 5\iff-5\le 2x-3\le 5$. Add 3: $-2\le 2x\le 8$. Divide by 2: $-1\le x\le 4$. Solution set $=[-1,4]$; the end points are included because the inequality is non-strict.

Solve $|x+1|>3$, write the answer in interval form and describe its graph on the number line. Model answer: $|x+1|>3$ means $x+1>3$ or $x+1<-3$, so $x>2$ or $x<-4$. Solution set $=(-\infty,-4)\cup(2,\infty)$. On the number line draw open circles at $-4$ and $2$, shading to the left of $-4$ and to the right of $2$; the segment between them is not shaded.

Define rational and irrational numbers. Express $0.\overline{4}$ and $1.2\overline{3}$ as fractions in lowest terms. Model answer: A rational number can be written $p/q$ with $p, q \in \mathbb{Z}$, $q \ne 0$; its decimal terminates or recurs. An irrational number cannot be so written; its decimal neither terminates nor recurs.

Write in interval notation and represent on a number line: (i) $-2 \le x < 3$, (ii) $x > 5$, (iii) $|x| \le 4$. Also find $(-5, 2] \cap [0, 6)$. Model answer: (i) $[-2, 3)$: solid dot at $-2$, hollow at $3$, segment shaded between. (ii) $(5, \infty)$: hollow dot at $5$, shading to the right. (iii) $|x| \le 4$ means $-4 \le x \le 4$, i.e. $[-4, 4]$: solid dots at both ends.
Solve $|3x - 2| < 4$ and express the solution as an interval. Model answer: $|3x-2| < 4$ means $-4 < 3x - 2 < 4$. Adding $2$: $-2 < 3x < 6$. Dividing by $3$:
Solve the pair $|x - 2| \le 3$ and $|x + 1| > 1$ simultaneously. Model answer: First inequality: $|x-2| \le 3 \Rightarrow -3 \le x-2 \le 3 \Rightarrow -1 \le x \le 5$, i.e. $[-1, 5]$.
State and prove the triangle inequality $|a+b| \le |a| + |b|$. Solve $|x - 2| + |x + 1| = 5$. Model answer: (b) The inside expressions vanish at $x = 2$ and $x = -1$, so split there.

Distinguish between accuracy and precision, giving one example of each. State what limits the precision of an instrument. Model answer: Outline: accuracy = closeness to the true value (a zero-error instrument is inaccurate); precision = closeness of repeated readings, set by the least count.

State the rules for counting significant figures. Hence give the number of significant figures in (i) $0.00602$, (ii) $6.023\times10^{23}$, (iii) $4.700\ \text{m}$. Model answer: (i) 3 — leading zeros do not count. (ii) 4 — only the mantissa $6.023$ counts. (iii) 4 — the trailing zeros follow a decimal point.

The length, breadth and thickness of a metal block are $5.12\ \text{cm}$, $2.34\ \text{cm}$ and $1.05\ \text{cm}$. Calculate its volume to the correct number of significant figures. Model answer: $V = 5.12 \times 2.34 \times 1.05 = 12.57984\ \text{cm}^{3}$. The fewest significant figures among the factors is 3 (in $1.05$), so $V = 12.6\ \text{cm}^{3}$.

A physical quantity is given by $P = a^{3}b^{2}/(\sqrt{c}\,d)$. If the percentage errors in $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ are 1 %, 2 %, 3 % and 4 % respectively, find the maximum percentage error in $P$. Model answer: $\dfrac{\Delta P}{P}\times100 = 3(1) + 2(2) + \tfrac{1}{2}(3) + 1(4) = 3 + 4 + 1.5 + 4 = 12.5\ \%$.

State the principle of homogeneity of dimensions and describe three uses of dimensional analysis. The value of the gravitational constant is $G = 6.67\times10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{kg}^{-2}$ in SI units. State the parallelogram law of vector addition and derive expressions for the magnitude and direction of the resultant of two vectors. Model answer: Outline: state the law, then reproduce the derivation of $R = \sqrt{P^{2}+Q^{2}+2PQ\cos\theta}$ and $\tan\alpha = Q\sin\theta/(P+Q\cos\theta)$ given in §2.1.

Define a unit vector. If $\vec{A} = 3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + 12\hat{k}$, find its magnitude, the unit vector along it and its direction cosines. Model answer: $A = \sqrt{9 + 16 + 144} = \sqrt{169} = 13$. $\hat{A} = (3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + 12\hat{k})/13$; direction cosines $l = 3/13 = 0.231$, $m = -4/13 = -0.308$, $n = 12/13 = 0.923$.

Two forces of $6\ \text{N}$ and $8\ \text{N}$ act on a body at right angles to each other. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant force. Model answer: $R = \sqrt{6^{2}+8^{2}} = 10\ \text{N}$; $\tan\alpha = 8/6 = 1.333$, so $\alpha = 53.1^{\circ}$ from the $6\ \text{N}$ force.

Distinguish between the scalar and the vector product of two vectors, giving one physical example of each. Model answer: Outline: use the comparison table in §2.3 — scalar versus vector result, $\cos\theta$ versus $\sin\theta$, order dependence; work and torque as examples.

Find the angle between the vectors $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = 6\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$. Model answer: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 12 - 6 - 2 = 4$; $A = \sqrt{4+4+1} = 3$ and $B = \sqrt{36+9+4} = 7$. So $\cos\theta = 4/21 = 0.1905$ and $\theta = 79.0^{\circ}$.

State and explain the triangle, parallelogram and polygon laws of vector addition. Two forces $P$ and $Q$ act at a point. Show that the resultant is maximum when they are parallel and minimum when they are antiparallel. Model answer: (b) $R^{2} = P^{2}+Q^{2}+2PQ\cos\theta$ increases with $\cos\theta$, which is greatest ($+1$) at $\theta = 0^{\circ}$, giving $R_{\max} = P+Q$, and least ($-1$) at $\theta = 180^{\circ}$, giving $R_{\min} = P-Q$. Then $P + Q = 14$ and $P - Q = 2$, so $P = 8\ \text{N}$ and $Q = 6\ \text{N}$.

Define the scalar and vector products and state two properties of each. Given $\vec{A} = 4\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}$ and $\vec{B} = 2\hat{i} + 5\hat{j}$, find $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}$, $\vec{A}\times\vec{B}$, the angle between the Model answer: (b) $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = (4)(2) + (3)(5) = 23$. $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = (4\times5 - 3\times2)\hat{k} = 14\hat{k}$, of magnitude 14. $A = 5$, $B = \sqrt{29} = 5.385$, so $\cos\theta = 23/26.93 = 0.854$ and $\theta = 31.3^{\circ}$. Area of the triangle $= \frac{1}{2}(14) = 7$ square units.

A car accelerates uniformly from rest and covers $100\ \text{m}$ in $5\ \text{s}$. Find its acceleration and the distance covered in the $5^{\text{th}}$ second. Model answer: From $s = ut+\frac12at^2$ with $u=0$: $100 = \frac12a(25)$, so $a = 8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. Then $s_5 = u + \frac{a}{2}(2\times5-1) = 0 + 4(9) = 36\ \text{m}$.

Define linear momentum and impulse. Show that the impulse of a force equals the change of momentum it produces, and explain why a long-jump pit is filled with sand. Model answer: Outline: state both definitions, derive $J = mv - mu$ from $F = dp/dt$, and note that sand lengthens $\Delta t$ so $F_{av} = \Delta p/\Delta t$ falls.

A bullet of mass $10\ \text{g}$ is fired from a gun of mass $5\ \text{kg}$ with a muzzle velocity of $300\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Calculate the recoil velocity of the gun. Model answer: Total momentum before firing is zero, so $0 = (0.010)(300) + 5V$, giving $V = -0.6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$: the gun recoils at $0.6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

Two masses of $6\ \text{kg}$ and $4\ \text{kg}$ hang from the ends of a light string over a smooth pulley. Find the acceleration of the system and the tension in the string. Take $g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. Model answer: $a = \dfrac{(6-4)(10)}{6+4} = 2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ and $T = \dfrac{2(6)(4)(10)}{10} = 48\ \text{N}$.

A uniform metre rule of weight $2\ \text{N}$ balances on a knife edge at the $30\ \text{cm}$ mark when a weight $W$ hangs at the $10\ \text{cm}$ mark. Find $W$ and the reaction at the knife edge. Model answer: The weight of the uniform rule acts at the $50\ \text{cm}$ mark, $20\ \text{cm}$ right of the knife edge, while $W$ hangs $20\ \text{cm}$ to the left. Moments about the knife edge give $W \times 20 = 2 \times 20$, so $W = 2\ \text{N}$, and the reaction is $R = 2 + 2 = 4\ \text{N}$ upwards.

State Newton's second law of motion and use it to derive $F = ma$, explaining why this form fails for a body of changing mass. (ii) $f_k = 0.4 \times 50 = 20\ \text{N}$, so $a = (25-20)/5 = 1\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

Define work, energy and power, and state their SI units. Show that the work done by a variable force is the area under the force–displacement graph. Model answer: , 2., 3. See §5.1, the derivation box in §5.3, and the comparison table in §5.5.

A car of mass $1000\ \text{kg}$ moves up an incline of $1$ in $20$ at a steady $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ against a frictional resistance of $200\ \text{N}$. Calculate the power developed by the engine. Take $g = 10\ \text{m Model answer: At steady speed the driving force balances gravity component plus friction: $F = mg\sin\theta + R = 1000 \times 10 \times \frac{1}{20} + 200 = 500 + 200 = 700\ \text{N}$. Then $P = Fv = 700 \times 20 = 14000\ \text{W} = 14\ \text{kW}$.

A spring of force constant $200\ \text{N m}^{-1}$ is compressed by $0.10\ \text{m}$ and used to push a block of mass $0.50\ \text{kg}$ along a frictionless table. Find the elastic potential energy stored and the speed of Model answer: $U = \frac{1}{2}kx^{2} = \frac{1}{2}(200)(0.10)^{2} = 1.0\ \text{J}$. All of it becomes kinetic energy: $\frac{1}{2}(0.50)v^{2} = 1.0$, so $v^{2} = 4.0$ and $v = 2.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

State the principle of conservation of energy. Show that for a body falling freely from a height $H$ the sum of its kinetic and potential energies is the same at every point of the fall. Model answer: (b) See §5.4: at height $h$, $v^{2} = 2g(H-h)$ so $K = mg(H-h)$ while $U = mgh$, giving $K+U = mgH$ everywhere. (c) The stone has fallen $45 - 20 = 25\ \text{m}$, so $K = mg(H-h) = 0.5 \times 10 \times 25 = 125\ \text{J}$ and $v = \sqrt{2K/m} = \sqrt{500} = 22.4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

(b) $v = \dfrac{5 \times 4 + 0}{5+3} = 2.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. $K_i = \frac{1}{2}(5)(16) = 40\ \text{J}$, $K_f = \frac{1}{2}(8)(2.5)^{2} = 25\

A stone of mass $0.20\ \text{kg}$ is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius $0.50\ \text{m}$ at $4\ \text{rev s}^{-1}$. Calculate its linear speed and the tension in the string. Model answer: $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi(4) = 8\pi = 25.13\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$. Linear speed $v = r\omega = 0.50 \times 25.13 = 12.6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Tension $= mr\omega^{2} = 0.20 \times 0.50 \times (25.13)^{2} = 0.10 \times 631.7 = 63.2\ \text{N}$.

What is meant by banking of a road? Derive an expression for the angle of banking of a curved road for a vehicle moving with speed $v$ on a curve of radius $r$. A cyclist rides round a circular track of radius $20\ \text Model answer: (b) A leaning cyclist obeys the same relation, $\tan\theta = v^{2}/rg = 100/(20 \times 10) = 0.50$, so $\theta = 26.6^{\circ}$ from the vertical.

Derive expressions for the minimum speeds at the highest and lowest points for a body to just complete a vertical circle of radius $r$. A bucket of water of mass $2\ \text{kg}$ is whirled in a vertical circle of radius $ Model answer: (b) Minimum speed at the top: $v_1 = \sqrt{gr} = \sqrt{10 \times 1} = 3.16\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Then $v_2^{2} = v_1^{2} + 4gr = 10 + 40 = 50$, so $T_2 = \dfrac{mv_2^{2}}{r} + mg = \dfrac{2 \times 50}{1} + 20 = 120\ \text{N}$ (which is $6mg$, as expected when $T_1 = 0$).
State Newton's law of gravitation. Define $G$ and give its SI unit and dimensional formula. Model answer: , 2., 3., 4. See §7.1, §7.3, the depth derivation in §7.4 and §7.5.

Calculate the height and orbital speed of a geostationary satellite. ($g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, $R = 6.4\times10^{6}\ \text{m}$.) Model answer: $GM = gR^{2} = 4.01\times10^{14}$. With $T = 86400\ \text{s}$, $r = \left(GMT^{2}/4\pi^{2}\right)^{1/3} = \left(7.59\times10^{22}\right)^{1/3} = 4.23\times10^{7}\ \text{m}$. Height $h = r - R = 3.59\times10^{7}\ \text{m} \approx 36\,000\ \text{km}$; speed $v = 2\pi r/T = 3.08\times10^{3}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

Two spheres, each of mass $100\ \text{kg}$, have their centres $1.0\ \text{m}$ apart. Find the gravitational force between them and comment on its size. Model answer: $F = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^{2}} = \dfrac{6.67\times10^{-11}\times100\times100}{1.0^{2}} = 6.67\times10^{-7}\ \text{N}$ — about the weight of a grain of dust. Gravity is negligible between everyday objects and matters only when one mass is astronomically large.

Define escape velocity and derive the expression $v_e = \sqrt{2gR}$. Show that the escape velocity is $\sqrt{2}$ times the orbital velocity of a satellite close to the planet's surface. Model answer: (c) $v_e = \sqrt{2g_mR_m} = \sqrt{2\times1.62\times1.74\times10^{6}} = \sqrt{5.64\times10^{6}} = 2.37\times10^{3}\ \text{m s}^{-1} = 2.37\ \text{km s}^{-1}$. This is of the same order as the speeds of gas molecules at lunar surface temperatures, so over time all the gas has escaped.

Derive expressions for the orbital velocity and the time period of a satellite revolving at a height $h$ above the Earth's surface, and hence obtain Kepler's third law. What is a geostationary satellite? State the condit Model answer: See the derivation box in §7.6 and the four conditions listed in §7.9.

Obtain expressions for the kinetic energy, potential energy and total energy of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius $r$, and explain the significance of the negative sign of the total energy. A satellite of mass $5 Model answer: (b) $r = R+h = 6.4\times10^{6} + 3.6\times10^{6} = 1.0\times10^{7}\ \text{m}$, $GM = gR^{2} = 4.01\times10^{14}$. Binding energy $= \dfrac{GMm}{2r} = \dfrac{4.01\times10^{14}\times500}{2\times1.0\times10^{7}} = 1.0\times10^{10}\ \text{J}$.

Define Young modulus. A steel wire $3.0\ \text{m}$ long with cross-sectional area $2.0\ \text{mm}^{2}$ stretches by $1.5\ \text{mm}$ under a load $W$. Find $W$, given $Y = 2.0\times10^{11}\ \text{Pa}$. Model answer: $F = \dfrac{YAe}{L} = \dfrac{2.0\times10^{11}\times2.0\times10^{-6}\times1.5\times10^{-3}}{3.0} = 200\ \text{N}$.

Define bulk modulus and compressibility. The pressure on a sample of water is increased by $4.4\times10^{7}\ \text{Pa}$. Find the percentage decrease in its volume if $B = 2.2\times10^{9}\ \text{Pa}$. Model answer: $\dfrac{\Delta V}{V} = \dfrac{p}{B} = \dfrac{4.4\times10^{7}}{2.2\times10^{9}} = 0.020$, i.e. a decrease of $2.0\ \%$.

Show that the energy stored per unit volume of a stretched wire is $\frac{1}{2}\times$ stress $\times$ strain. A wire of volume $1.0\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}^{3}$ is stretched so that its strain is $1.0\times10^{-3}$. Find Model answer: Outline: work done $= \int_0^e (YA/L)x\,dx = \frac{1}{2}Fe$; divide by volume $AL$ to get $u = \frac{1}{2}(F/A)(e/L)$. Numerically $U = \frac{1}{2}Y\varepsilon^{2}V = \frac{1}{2}\times2.0\times10^{11}\times(1.0\times10^{-3})^{2}\times1.0\times10^{-6} = 0.10\ \text{J}$.

Define the three elastic moduli and write the expression for each. Derive an expression for the elastic potential energy stored in a stretched wire and hence for the energy per unit volume. Model answer: (c) $F = YAe/L = (1.1\times10^{11}\times1.0\times10^{-6}\times1.0\times10^{-3})/2.0 = 55\ \text{N}$, so $U = \frac{1}{2}Fe = \frac{1}{2}\times55\times1.0\times10^{-3} = 2.75\times10^{-2}\ \text{J}$.

A copper wire and a steel wire, each $2.0\ \text{m}$ long and $1.0\ \text{mm}$ in diameter, are joined end to end and a force of $100\ \text{N}$ is applied to the free ends. Given $Y_{Cu} = 1.1\times10^{11}\ \text{Pa}$ a Model answer: The two wires are in series, so each carries the same force $100\ \text{N}$ and, having the same diameter, the same stress.

Distinguish between heat and temperature on a molecular basis. Explain why a bucket of warm water can hold more thermal energy than a small flame at a much higher temperature. Model answer: Outline: temperature = average molecular KE (an intensive quantity, per molecule); heat = energy in transit driven by a temperature difference. Thermal energy is the total molecular KE, so it grows with the number of molecules — a bucket of water has of order $10^{27}$ molecules against a flame's tiny number, so the to

The mercury thread in a thermometer is $4.0\ \text{cm}$ long at the ice point and $24.0\ \text{cm}$ long at the steam point. Find Model answer: (a) $t = \dfrac{13.0-4.0}{24.0-4.0}\times100 = \dfrac{9.0}{20.0}\times100 = 45\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$. (b) $l = 4.0 + 0.65\times20.0 = 17.0\ \text{cm}$.

Calculate the average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule at $127\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$, and find the temperature in $^{\circ}$C at which it is half this value. Model answer: $T = 127+273 = 400\ \text{K}$, so $\bar{E}_k = 1.5\times1.38\times10^{-23}\times400 = 8.28\times10^{-21}\ \text{J}$. Half of this needs $T = 200\ \text{K} = -73\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Define thermometric property and name the property used in a constant volume gas thermometer and in a platinum resistance thermometer. A faulty thermometer reads $2\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$ in melting ice and $102\ ^{\circ}\te Model answer: (a) A thermometric property is any measurable physical property that varies continuously, uniformly and reproducibly with temperature. Gas thermometer: the pressure of a fixed mass of gas at constant volume. Platinum thermometer: the electrical resistance of the platinum wire.

A glass flask of volume $500\ \text{cm}^{3}$ is completely filled with mercury at $0\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$. On heating to $80\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$, $6.0\ \text{cm}^{3}$ of mercury overflows. If $\gamma_{\text{Hg}} = 1.8\times Model answer: $\gamma_a = \dfrac{6.0}{500\times80} = 1.5\times10^{-4}\ \text{K}^{-1}$. Then $\gamma_g = \gamma_r - \gamma_a = 1.8\times10^{-4} - 1.5\times10^{-4} = 3.0\times10^{-5}\ \text{K}^{-1}$, so $\alpha_g = \gamma_g/3 = 1.0\times10^{-5}\ \text{K}^{-1}$.

A brass scale is correct at $15\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$. It is used at $35\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$ and reads a length of $50.00\ \text{cm}$. What is the true length? Take $\alpha_{\text{brass}} = 1.9\times10^{-5}\ \text{K}^{-1}$. Model answer: At $35\ ^{\circ}$C each scale division has grown, so every division now measures more than it claims. True length $= 50.00\left(1 + 1.9\times10^{-5}\times20\right) = 50.00(1+3.8\times10^{-4}) = 50.019\ \text{cm}$.

An iron rim of diameter $79.80\ \text{cm}$ at $20\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$ is to be fitted on a wooden cart wheel of diameter $80.00\ \text{cm}$. To what temperature must the rim be heated? Take $\alpha_{\text{iron}} = 1.2\tim Model answer: (a) The rim must expand from $79.80$ to $80.00\ \text{cm}$, so $\Delta d = 0.20\ \text{cm}$ and

State Newton's law of cooling and show that the temperature of a cooling body falls exponentially towards that of its surroundings. Model answer: Outline: state the law; write $dQ/dt = -K(\theta-\theta_0)$; put $dQ = mc\,d\theta$ to get $d\theta/dt = -k(\theta-\theta_0)$; separate variables and integrate to $\ln(\theta-\theta_0) = -kt + C$; apply $\theta=\theta_1$ at $t=0$ to obtain $\theta = \theta_0 + (\theta_1-\theta_0)e^{-kt}$.

A block of copper of mass 0.4 kg at $100\ ^\circ$C is dropped into 0.2 kg of water at $20\ ^\circ$C in a container of negligible heat capacity. Find the final temperature. ($c_{Cu}=400$, $c_w=4200\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\text{ Model answer: Heat lost $= 0.4\times400\times(100-\theta) = 160(100-\theta)$; heat gained $= 0.2\times4200\times(\theta-20) = 840(\theta-20)$. So $16\,000-160\theta = 840\theta-16\,800$, giving $1000\theta = 32\,800$ and $\theta = 32.8\ ^\circ$C.

Define specific latent heat of fusion and of vaporisation, and explain why $L_v$ is much larger than $L_f$ for the same substance. Model answer: Definitions as in §11.4. $L_v > L_f$ because melting only has to loosen the lattice enough for molecules to slide, whereas vaporisation must separate the molecules completely against their mutual attraction and, in addition, do work pushing back the atmosphere as the vapour expands.

Define specific latent heat of vaporisation. Describe, with the necessary theory and two precautions, how the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is measured by the method of mixtures. Model answer: (a) The heat needed to change unit mass of a liquid into vapour at its boiling point without any change of temperature. (b) Steam from a boiler passes through a steam trap into a weighed calorimeter holding a known mass of cold water; record $\theta_1$, pass steam until the rise is about $20\ ^\circ$C, record $\theta_2

Define thermal conductivity and derive $H = kA(\theta_1-\theta_2)/L$ for steady conduction through a slab. Why must the slab be lagged? Model answer: Outline: define $k$ as in §12.1; state $H \propto A$ and $H \propto \Delta\theta/L$ in the steady state; combine to $H = kA\Delta\theta/L$. Lagging ensures no heat escapes through the sides, so the heat current is the same at every cross-section and the gradient is uniform.

Then $H = \Delta\theta/R = 20/0.100 = 200$ W. Junction temperature $\theta = 25 - HR_1 = 25 - 200\times0.020 = 21\ ^\circ$C. (Check: $(21-5)/0.080 = 200$ W.)

Distinguish between natural and forced convection, and explain why a thermos flask has a vacuum between its walls and silvered surfaces. Model answer: Natural convection is driven by the density change of the fluid itself in a gravitational field; forced convection is driven by an external pump or fan and is much faster.
