Model answer: $A = 20\times10^{-4} = 2.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2$, $T = 800$ K, $T_0 = 300$ K. $T^4 - T_0^4 = 4.096\times10^{11} - 8.1\times10^{9} = 4.015\times10^{11}$. So $P = 5.67\times10^{-8}\times2.0\times10^{-3}\times4.015\times10^{11} = 45.5$ W.

State two reasons why the method is unsuitable for glass. State the assumptions of the kinetic molecular model of an ideal gas, and explain on this model what pressure and temperature mean. Model answer: The six assumptions of §13.3. Pressure is the average force per unit area from molecular bombardment of the walls; temperature is a direct measure of the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules, $\overline{E} = \frac{3}{2}kT$.

Define the Boltzmann constant and show that the average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule is $\frac{3}{2}kT$. Model answer: Define $k = R/N_A$. Then from kinetic theory $pV = \frac{1}{3}mN\overline{c^{2}} = \frac{2}{3}N(\frac{1}{2}m\overline{c^{2}})$; equating to $pV = NkT$ gives $\frac{1}{2}m\overline{c^{2}} = \frac{3}{2}kT$.

Derive Mayer's relation $C_p - C_v = R$ and hence find $\gamma$ for a monatomic gas. Model answer: Derivation as in §13.7. For a monatomic gas $C_v = \frac{3}{2}R$, so $C_p = C_v + R = \frac{5}{2}R$ and $\gamma = \frac{5}{2}R \div \frac{3}{2}R = 5/3 = 1.67$.

State the assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases and derive the expression $p = \frac{1}{3}\rho\overline{c^{2}}$ for the pressure of an ideal gas. Hence show that the average translational kinetic energy of a molecul Model answer: Full derivation as set out in §13.4, Steps 1 to 6, followed by the argument of §13.5.

A vessel of volume $0.0249\ \text{m}^3$ contains oxygen at 300 K and a pressure of $1.0\times10^{5}\ \text{Pa}$. Taking $M = 32\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$, find Model answer: (a) $n = pV/RT = (1.0\times10^{5}\times0.0249)/(8.314\times300) = 2490/2494 = 1.00$ mol.

Distinguish between a real image and a virtual image, giving one example of each from everyday life. Model answer: Real: rays actually meet, screen-catchable, inverted, formed in front of the mirror (the image on a cinema screen, or on the film of a reflecting telescope). Virtual: only the backward extensions meet, not screen-catchable, erect, formed behind the mirror (your face in a plane or convex mirror).

Show that the focal length of a spherical mirror is half its radius of curvature for paraxial rays. Model answer: See the derivation in §14.1: $PC \approx h/\theta$, $PF \approx h/2\theta$, hence $f = R/2$.

State the new Cartesian sign convention and use it to explain why the focal length of a convex mirror is taken as positive. Model answer: Rules as in §14.2. Light is drawn travelling left to right and strikes the convex surface from the left; its focus lies behind the mirror, i.e. further along the direction of the incident light, so $PF$ is a positive distance and $f > 0$.

Using the principle of reversibility of light, show that ${}_1n_2 = 1/{}_2n_1$, and hence prove ${}_1n_2 \times {}_2n_3 \times {}_3n_1 = 1$. Model answer: See §15.2 (b) and (c). Reversing the ray interchanges $i$ and $r$, so ${}_2n_1 = \sin r/\sin i = 1/{}_1n_2$. Writing each relative index as a ratio of absolute indices, ${}_1n_2\,{}_2n_3\,{}_3n_1 = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1}\cdot\dfrac{n_3}{n_2}\cdot\dfrac{n_1}{n_3} = 1$.

Calculate the angle of minimum deviation of an equilateral prism made of glass of refractive index $1.6$. Model answer: $\sin\left(\dfrac{60^{\circ}+\delta_m}{2}\right) = 1.6\sin30^{\circ} = 0.8$, so $\dfrac{60^{\circ}+\delta_m}{2} = 53.13^{\circ}$ and $\delta_m = 106.26^{\circ} - 60^{\circ} = 46.26^{\circ} \approx 46.3^{\circ}$.

The angle of minimum deviation of a prism of refracting angle $60^{\circ}$ is $40^{\circ}$. Find the refractive index of its material and the angle of incidence at minimum deviation. Model answer: $n = \dfrac{\sin\left(\frac{60^{\circ}+40^{\circ}}{2}\right)}{\sin 30^{\circ}} = \dfrac{\sin 50^{\circ}}{0.5} = \dfrac{0.7660}{0.5} = 1.532$. The angle of incidence is $i = \dfrac{A+\delta_m}{2} = 50^{\circ}$.

Define the power of a lens and its unit. Two thin lenses of powers $+5\ \text{D}$ and $-3\ \text{D}$ are placed in contact. Find the focal length of the combination and state whether it converges or diverges. Model answer: $P = P_1 + P_2 = 5 - 3 = +2\ \text{D}$, so $F = 1/2 = 0.5\ \text{m} = 50\ \text{cm}$. The power is positive, so the combination converges.

Define angular magnification and show that, for a simple microscope with the final image at the least distance of distinct vision, $M = 1 + D/f$. Model answer: See the derivation in §17.3 — the marks are for $M = \beta/\alpha = D/u_0$, for substituting $v = -D$ in the lens formula, and for the final step $D/u_0 = 1 + D/f$.

State the principle of quantisation and conservation of charge. How many electrons must be removed from a body to give it a charge of $+2\ \mu\text{C}$? Model answer: $n = \dfrac{q}{e} = \dfrac{2\times10^{-6}}{1.6\times10^{-19}} = 1.25\times10^{13}$ electrons must be removed.

Two point charges $+9\ \mu\text{C}$ and $-4\ \mu\text{C}$ are placed $1\ \text{m}$ apart in air. Locate the point where the resultant electric field is zero. Model answer: The point lies beyond the $-4\ \mu\text{C}$ charge. With $d$ measured from it, $9/(1+d)^{2} = 4/d^{2}$ gives $3d = 2+2d$, so $d = 2\ \text{m}$ — that is, $3\ \text{m}$ from the $+9\ \mu\text{C}$ charge on the side away from it.

A charge of $17.7\ \mu\text{C}$ is placed at the centre of a cube of side $10\ \text{cm}$. Calculate the electric flux through one face of the cube. Model answer: Total flux $= q/\varepsilon_0 = 17.7\times10^{-6}/8.85\times10^{-12} = 2.0\times10^{6}\ \text{N m}^{2}\text{C}^{-1}$. One face gets one sixth: $3.33\times10^{5}\ \text{N m}^{2}\text{C}^{-1}$. The side length is irrelevant.

A metal sphere of radius $5\ \text{cm}$ carries a charge of $2\ \mu\text{C}$. Find the field at $2\ \text{cm}$, at $5\ \text{cm}$ and at $10\ \text{cm}$ from its centre. Model answer: At $2\ \text{cm}$ (inside): $E = 0$. At the surface: $E = 9\times10^{9}\times2\times10^{-6}/(0.05)^{2} = 7.2\times10^{6}\ \text{N C}^{-1}$. At $10\ \text{cm}$: $E = 9\times10^{9}\times2\times10^{-6}/(0.10)^{2} = 1.8\times10^{6}\ \text{N C}^{-1}$.

concepts.t: Calculate the work done in moving a charge of $2\ \mu\text{C}$ from a point $10\ \text{cm}$ away from a charge of $+3\ \mu\text{C}$ to a point $5\ \text{cm}$ away from it. Model answer: $V_1 = \dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times3\times10^{-6}}{0.10} = 2.7\times10^{5}\ \text{V}$ and $V_2 = \dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times3\times10^{-6}}{0.05} = 5.4\times10^{5}\ \text{V}$. The work done by the external agent is $W = q(V_2 - V_1) = 2\times10^{-6}\times2.7\times10^{5} = 0.54\ \text{J}$.

concepts.t: An electron initially at rest is accelerated through a potential difference of $1000\ \text{V}$. Find its final kinetic energy in joules and its speed. Model answer: $KE = eV = 1.6\times10^{-19}\times1000 = 1.6\times10^{-16}\ \text{J}$ (that is $1\ \text{keV}$). Then $v = \sqrt{2\times1.6\times10^{-16}/9.1\times10^{-31}} = \sqrt{3.52\times10^{14}} = 1.88\times10^{7}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

Model answer: Charge is conserved: $V = \dfrac{C_1V_1}{C_1+C_2} = \dfrac{2\times100}{5} = 40\ \text{V}$. $U_i = \frac12(2\times10^{-6})(100)^{2} = 1.0\times10^{-2}\ \text{J}$; $U_f = \frac12(5\times10^{-6})(40)^{2} = 4.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{J}$. Find the equivalent resistance, the current Model answer: Parallel part: $4\times12/16 = 3\ \Omega$; total $= 2+3 = 5\ \Omega$. Current drawn $I = 10/5 = 2\ \text{A}$. Pd across the parallel part $= 2\times3 = 6\ \text{V}$, so $I_4 = 6/4 = 1.5\ \text{A}$ and $I_{12} = 6/12 = 0.5\ \text{A}$ (sum $= 2\ \text{A}$, as it must be).

A cell of emf $2.0\ \text{V}$ and internal resistance $0.5\ \Omega$ is connected across a $4.5\ \Omega$ resistor. Find the current, the terminal potential difference, and the power dissipated in the external resistor. Model answer: $I = E/(R+r) = 2.0/5.0 = 0.40\ \text{A}$; $V = IR = 0.40\times4.5 = 1.8\ \text{V}$ (or $E - Ir = 2.0-0.2$); $P = I^{2}R = 0.16\times4.5 = 0.72\ \text{W}$.

In a metre bridge experiment the unknown resistance $X$ is in the left gap and a $6\ \Omega$ resistance box in the right gap. The balance point is at $40\ \text{cm}$ from the left end. Find $X$, and state where the balan Model answer: $X = R\,l/(100-l) = 6\times40/60 = 4\ \Omega$. On interchanging, the balance length measured from the left end becomes $100-40 = 60\ \text{cm}$, since now $R/X = l'/(100-l')$ gives $6/4 = 60/40$.

State Kirchhoff's laws of electrical networks and name the conservation principle behind each. Draw a Wheatstone bridge and derive its balance condition. Model answer: (a), 1.(b), 2.(a), 2.(b), 3.(a) are bookwork: see the boxed statements in §23.4, the Wheatstone derivation, §23.6 and §23.7.

Show that the density of a nucleus is independent of its mass number, and calculate its value. Take $R_0 = 1.2\ \text{fm}$ and $m_n = 1.67\times10^{-27}\ \text{kg}$. Model answer: $\rho = 3m_n/4\pi R_0^{3}$; numerically $3(1.67\times10^{-27})/[4\pi(1.2\times10^{-15})^{3}] = 5.01\times10^{-27}/7.24\times10^{-45} = 2.3\times10^{17}\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$.

Model answer: $\Delta m = 3(1.007825) + 4(1.008665) - 7.016004 = 3.023475 + 4.034660 - 7.016004 = 0.042131\ \text{u}$. $B = 0.042131\times931.5 = 39.2\ \text{MeV}$, so $B/A = 39.2/7 = 5.6\ \text{MeV per nucleon}$.

Explain qualitatively how the discrete energy levels of isolated atoms become energy bands in a solid. Why does the resistance of a metal increase but that of a semiconductor decrease with rise in temperature? Model answer: Outline: in a metal the carrier number is fixed, so more violent lattice vibrations scatter electrons more and $\rho$ rises. In a semiconductor the carrier number grows like $e^{-E_g/2kT}$; this exponential increase dominates the extra scattering, so $\rho$ falls (negative temperature coefficient).

Using dimensional analysis, derive an expression for the time period $T$ of a simple pendulum, assuming it depends on its length $l$, the mass $m$ of the bob and the acceleration due to gravity $g$. State one limitation Model answer: Let $T = k\,l^{a}m^{b}g^{c}$. Dimensions: $[T] = T$, $[l] = L$, $[m] = M$, $[g] = LT^{-2}$. So $T^{1}= L^{a}M^{b}L^{c}T^{-2c}$. Comparing: $M$: $b = 0$; $T$: $-2c = 1$ so $c = -\tfrac12$; $L$: $a + c = 0$ so $a = \tfrac12$. Hence $T = k\sqrt{l/g}$, independent of mass. Limitation: the dimensionless constant $k$ ($= 2\p

Two forces of $10\ \text{N}$ and $6\ \text{N}$ act at a point with an angle of $60^{\circ}$ between them. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant. Model answer: $R = \sqrt{P^{2} + Q^{2} + 2PQ\cos\theta} = \sqrt{100 + 36 + 2(10)(6)(0.5)} = \sqrt{196} = 14\ \text{N}$. Direction from the $10\ \text{N}$ force: $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P + Q\cos\theta} = \dfrac{6(0.866)}{10 + 3} = 0.400$, so $\alpha \approx 21.8^{\circ}$.

A ball is projected with a speed of $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $30^{\circ}$ above the horizontal ($g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$). Find the time of flight, the maximum height and the horizontal range. Model answer: $T = \dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g} = \dfrac{2(20)(0.5)}{10} = 2.0\ \text{s}$. $H = \dfrac{u^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}{2g} = \dfrac{400(0.25)}{20} = 5.0\ \text{m}$. $R = \dfrac{u^{2}\sin2\theta}{g} = \dfrac{400(0.866)}{10} = 34.6\ \text{m}$.

A gun of mass $5\ \text{kg}$ fires a bullet of mass $20\ \text{g}$ at $400\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. State the principle you use and find the recoil velocity of the gun. Model answer: Principle: conservation of linear momentum (no external horizontal force). $0 = m_bv_b + Mv_g$, so $v_g = -\dfrac{m_bv_b}{M} = -\dfrac{0.020\times400}{5} = -1.6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$: the gun recoils at $1.6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ opposite to the bullet.

State the laws of solid friction. A $20\ \text{kg}$ block rests on a horizontal floor with $\mu = 0.3$. Find the horizontal force needed to move it at constant speed ($g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$). Model answer: Laws: (i) friction opposes relative motion; (ii) limiting friction is independent of the area of contact; (iii) $F \propto R$, $F = \mu R$; (iv) kinetic friction is less than limiting friction and independent of speed. $R = mg = 20\times9.8 = 196\ \text{N}$; $F = \mu R = 0.3\times196 = 58.8\ \text{N}$.

A $2\ \text{kg}$ body is released from rest at a height of $20\ \text{m}$ ($g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$). Using energy, find its speed when it is $5\ \text{m}$ above the ground, and show that the total energy there equals t Model answer: Fall of $15\ \text{m}$: $v^{2} = 2gh = 2(10)(15) = 300$, so $v = 17.3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. At $5\ \text{m}$: $K = \tfrac12(2)(300) = 300\ \text{J}$, $U = mgh = 2(10)(5) = 100\ \text{J}$, total $400\ \text{J}$. Initially $U = 2(10)(20) = 400\ \text{J}$, $K = 0$. Equal, so mechanical energy is conserved.

Derive an expression for the acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ above the Earth's surface. Find $g$ at a height $R/2$ ($g_0 = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$). Model answer: At the surface $g_0 = GM/R^{2}$. At height $h$: $g = \dfrac{GM}{(R+h)^{2}}$, so $g = g_0\left(\dfrac{R}{R+h}\right)^{2} = g_0\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)^{-2}$. For $h = R/2$: $g = 9.8\times\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^{2} = 9.8\times\dfrac{4}{9} = 4.36\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

A car of mass $1000\ \text{kg}$ rounds a level curve of radius $50\ \text{m}$ at $10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Find the centripetal force, and the banking angle at which no friction is needed on this curve ($g = 10\ \text{m s}^ Model answer: $F = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r} = \dfrac{1000\times100}{50} = 2000\ \text{N}$. With banking, $\tan\theta = \dfrac{v^{2}}{rg} = \dfrac{100}{50\times10} = 0.2$, so $\theta = 11.3^{\circ}$.

A steel wire $2\ \text{m}$ long with cross-section $1\ \text{mm}^{2}$ is stretched by $1\ \text{mm}$ by a force of $100\ \text{N}$. Find the Young modulus and the elastic energy stored. Model answer: $Y = \dfrac{FL}{A\,\Delta l} = \dfrac{100\times2}{(1\times10^{-6})(1\times10^{-3})} = 2\times10^{11}\ \text{N m}^{-2}$. Energy $= \tfrac12F\Delta l = \tfrac12(100)(10^{-3}) = 0.05\ \text{J}$.

Derive the three equations of uniformly accelerated motion using the velocity–time graph. A car accelerates uniformly from $10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ to $30\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in $200\ \text{m}$. Find the acceleration and the Model answer: (a) Draw a straight line AB on a $v$–$t$ graph from $v = u$ at $t = 0$ to $v = v$ at time $t$. Slope $= a$, so $a = \dfrac{v-u}{t}$, giving $v = u + at$. The displacement is the area under the line: a rectangle $ut$ plus a triangle $\tfrac12(v-u)t$, so $s = ut + \tfrac12(v-u)t = ut + \tfrac12at^{2}$, giving $s = ut + \

Derive an expression for the orbital speed and period of a satellite at height $h$ above the Earth. What is a geostationary satellite? State its conditions. Model answer: (a) Gravity supplies the centripetal force: $\dfrac{mv^{2}}{R+h} = \dfrac{GMm}{(R+h)^{2}}$, so $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{R+h}} = R\sqrt{\dfrac{g}{R+h}}$ (using $GM = gR^{2}$). Period $T = \dfrac{2\pi(R+h)}{v} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{(R+h)^{3}}{GM}}$. Both are independent of the satellite's mass. (b) A satellite that appears fix

Define linear, superficial and cubical expansivity. Show that $\gamma = 3\alpha$ for an isotropic solid. Model answer: $\alpha = \dfrac{\Delta l}{l\,\Delta\theta}$ (per unit length per kelvin); $\beta = \dfrac{\Delta A}{A\,\Delta\theta}$; $\gamma = \dfrac{\Delta V}{V\,\Delta\theta}$. A cube of side $l_0$: $V_0 = l_0^{3}$; at $\theta$, $l = l_0(1+\alpha\theta)$, so $V = l_0^{3}(1+\alpha\theta)^{3} \approx V_0(1 + 3\alpha\theta)$ (neglec

State Newton's law of cooling. A body cools from $80^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $60^{\circ}\text{C}$ in $10$ minutes in a room at $20^{\circ}\text{C}$. Estimate the time to cool from $60^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $40^{\circ}\text{C}$ Model answer: The rate of loss of heat of a body is proportional to the excess of its temperature over the surroundings (for small differences). First interval: mean excess $= 70 - 20 = 50$; fall $= 20$ in $10$ min, so rate $= 2.0\ \text{K min}^{-1}$ at $50\ \text{K}$ excess, i.e. $0.04\ \text{min}^{-1}$ per kelvin. Second interval:

A $0.5\ \text{kg}$ metal block at $100^{\circ}\text{C}$ is dropped into $0.4\ \text{kg}$ of water at $20^{\circ}\text{C}$ and the mixture reaches $30^{\circ}\text{C}$. Find the specific heat capacity of the metal ($c_w = Model answer: Heat lost by metal $=$ heat gained by water: $0.5\,c\,(100-30) = 0.4(4200)(30-20)$, so $35c = 16800$, $c = 480\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$.

Find the heat required to change $10\ \text{g}$ of ice at $-10^{\circ}\text{C}$ into steam at $100^{\circ}\text{C}$. ($c_{ice} = 2100$, $c_w = 4200\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, $L_f = 3.36\times10^{5}$, $L_v = 2.26\t Model answer: Ice warms $-10 \to 0$: $0.010\times2100\times10 = 210\ \text{J}$. Melts: $0.010\times3.36\times10^{5} = 3360\ \text{J}$. Water $0 \to 100$: $0.010\times4200\times100 = 4200\ \text{J}$. Boils: $0.010\times2.26\times10^{6} = 22\,600\ \text{J}$. Total $= 30\,370\ \text{J} \approx 3.0\times10^{4}\ \text{J}$.

Define thermal conductivity. Find the rate of heat flow through a glass pane of area $2\ \text{m}^{2}$ and thickness $0.1\ \text{m}$... use $k = 0.8\ \text{W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ with faces $20\ \text{K}$ apart. Model answer: Thermal conductivity $k$: the heat flowing per second through unit area of a slab of unit thickness when the faces differ by $1\ \text{K}$ (steady state), unit $\text{W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$. $H = \dfrac{kA\Delta\theta}{d} = \dfrac{0.8\times2\times20}{0.1} = 320\ \text{W}$.

State Stefan–Boltzmann's law. A black body of surface area $0.01\ \text{m}^{2}$ is at $727^{\circ}\text{C}$. Find the power radiated ($\sigma = 5.67\times10^{-8}\ \text{W m}^{-2}\text{K}^{-4}$). Model answer: The energy radiated per second by a black body is proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature and its area: $P = \sigma AT^{4}$. $T = 727 + 273 = 1000\ \text{K}$. $P = 5.67\times10^{-8}\times0.01\times10^{12} = 567\ \text{W}$.

State the zeroth law of thermodynamics and explain how it underlies the use of a thermometer. Model answer: If two bodies are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. A thermometer is the third body: when it reads the same for two bodies they have the same temperature and no net heat flows between them. In a mercury thermometer, the mercury reaches equilibrium with the body a

Calculate the volume of $2$ mol of an ideal gas at $27^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $1.013\times10^{5}\ \text{Pa}$ ($R = 8.31\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$). Model answer: $T = 300\ \text{K}$. $V = \dfrac{nRT}{P} = \dfrac{2\times8.31\times300}{1.013\times10^{5}} = 4.92\times10^{-2}\ \text{m}^{3} \approx 49\ \text{litres}$.

Derive the expression $P = \tfrac13\rho\overline{c^{2}}$ for the pressure of an ideal gas using the kinetic theory. Deduce that the mean kinetic energy of a molecule is $\tfrac32kT$. Model answer: (a) Take $N$ molecules, each of mass $m$, in a cubical box of side $l$. A molecule with velocity components $u_x, u_y, u_z$ strikes a wall perpendicular to $x$ and rebounds elastically; momentum change $= 2mu_x$. It returns to the same wall after time $2l/u_x$, so the rate of change of momentum (force) is $\dfrac{2mu_x

A coin lies at the bottom of a water tank $12\ \text{cm}$ deep. If $n_{water} = 4/3$, find the apparent depth. Explain why a pool looks shallower than it is. Model answer: $n = \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}$, so apparent depth $= \dfrac{12}{4/3} = 9\ \text{cm}$. Rays leaving the coin bend away from the normal on entering air, so to the eye they appear to come from a point nearer the surface.

Define the critical angle and total internal reflection. Find the critical angle for glass of refractive index $1.5$. Model answer: The critical angle is the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the refracted ray grazes the interface (angle of refraction $90^{\circ}$). Total internal reflection occurs when light travelling in the denser medium meets the boundary at an angle greater than $C$. $\sin C = \dfrac{1}{n} = \dfrac{1}{1.5} = 0.

A prism of angle $60^{\circ}$ and refractive index $\sqrt{2}$ is used. Find the angle of minimum deviation. Model answer: $n = \dfrac{\sin\frac{A+D}{2}}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}$. $\sin\dfrac{60+D}{2} = \sqrt{2}\sin30^{\circ} = 0.7071$, so $\dfrac{60+D}{2} = 45^{\circ}$ and $D = 30^{\circ}$.

An object is $30\ \text{cm}$ from a convex lens of focal length $20\ \text{cm}$. Find the image distance and magnification. Also find the power of a concave lens of focal length $25\ \text{cm}$. Model answer: $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{20} - \dfrac{1}{30} = \dfrac{1}{60}$, so $v = 60\ \text{cm}$ (real). $m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -2$ (inverted, twice the size). Power $P = \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{-0.25} = -4\ \text{D}$.

Define the dispersive power of a material. Find it for glass with $n_v = 1.532$, $n_r = 1.514$ and $n_y = 1.522$. Model answer: Dispersive power $\omega = \dfrac{n_v - n_r}{n_y - 1}$: the ratio of the angular dispersion to the mean deviation. $\omega = \dfrac{1.532 - 1.514}{1.522 - 1} = \dfrac{0.018}{0.522} = 0.0345$.

Draw the path of a ray through a prism and derive $n = \dfrac{\sin\frac{A+D}{2}}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}$. A ray falls on a prism of angle $60^{\circ}$ at $50^{\circ}$ and emerges at $50^{\circ}$. Find the deviation and the ref Model answer: (a) (Diagram: ray $PQ$ meets face $AB$ at $Q$, bends towards the normal, meets face $AC$ at $R$, emerges as $RS$ bending away; angles $i_1, r_1$ at $Q$ and $r_2, i_2$ at $R$; the deviation $D$ is between the incident ray $PQ$ extended and $RS$.) Deviation at the first face $= i_1 - r_1$; at the second $= i_2 - r_2$, so

Model answer: (Diagram: object $AB$ beyond $C$; ray $AD$ parallel to the axis reflects through $F$; ray $AP$ strikes the pole and reflects with equal angle; image $A'B'$ between $F$ and $C$.) Use the real-is-positive convention: $PB = u$, $PB' = v$, $PF = f$. The ray $AP$ hits the pole at angle $\theta$ and reflects at the same angl

State Coulomb's law. Find the force between two $2\ \mu\text{C}$ charges placed $3\ \text{cm}$ apart in air ($k = 9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^{2}\text{C}^{-2}$). Model answer: The force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, along the line joining them: $F = k\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^{2}}$. $F = \dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times(2\times10^{-6})^{2}}{(0.03)^{2}} = \dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times4\time

Define electric field intensity. Find the field at $0.30\ \text{m}$ from a point charge of $5\ \text{nC}$, and the force on a $2\ \text{nC}$ charge there. Model answer: The force per unit positive test charge at that point, $E = F/q$ (unit $\text{N C}^{-1}$). $E = \dfrac{kq}{r^{2}} = \dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times5\times10^{-9}}{0.09} = 500\ \text{N C}^{-1}$. $F = qE = 2\times10^{-9}\times500 = 1.0\times10^{-6}\ \text{N}$.

Define electric potential and the volt. Find the work done in taking a $2\ \mu\text{C}$ charge through a potential difference of $100\ \text{V}$. Model answer: Potential at a point is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing it from infinity to that point. One volt is one joule per coulomb. $W = qV = 2\times10^{-6}\times100 = 2\times10^{-4}\ \text{J}$.

Derive the energy stored in a capacitor. Find it for $10\ \mu\text{F}$ charged to $100\ \text{V}$. Model answer: Raising the charge on the plates from $q$ to $q + dq$ against the potential $V = q/C$ needs work $dW = \dfrac{q}{C}\,dq$. Total: $W = \int_0^Q\dfrac{q}{C}\,dq = \dfrac{Q^{2}}{2C} = \tfrac12CV^{2} = \tfrac12QV$. $U = \tfrac12(10\times10^{-6})(100)^{2} = 0.050\ \text{J}$.

A cell of emf $12\ \text{V}$ and internal resistance $1\ \Omega$ is connected to a $5\ \Omega$ resistor. Find the current, the terminal potential difference and the power dissipated in the external resistor. Model answer: $I = \dfrac{E}{R + r} = \dfrac{12}{6} = 2.0\ \text{A}$. Terminal p.d. $V = E - Ir = 12 - 2 = 10\ \text{V}$. $P = I^{2}R = 4\times5 = 20\ \text{W}$.

State Ohm's law and explain why it fails for a filament lamp. Find the resistance of a copper wire $2\ \text{m}$ long, $0.5\ \text{mm}^{2}$ in area ($\rho = 1.7\times10^{-8}\ \Omega\,\text{m}$). Model answer: Ohm's law: at constant temperature the current through a conductor is proportional to the potential difference across it. A filament heats up, so its resistance rises with current and the $V$–$I$ graph is not a straight line. $R = \dfrac{\rho l}{A} = \dfrac{1.7\times10^{-8}\times2}{0.5\times10^{-6}} = 0.068\ \Omega$.

Derive the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor, $C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}$. Show that the energy density is $\tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^{2}$. Model answer: (a) For large plates the field between them (area $A$, charge $\pm Q$) is $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} = \dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0A}$ (Gauss's law). The potential difference is $V = Ed = \dfrac{Qd}{\varepsilon_0A}$. By definition $C = \dfrac{Q}{V} = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}$. (b) $U = \tfrac12CV^{2} = \tfrac12\dfr

Define half-life and decay constant, and derive the relation between them. Model answer: Half-life $T_{1/2}$: the time in which half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample decay. Decay constant $\lambda$: the probability of decay of a nucleus per unit time (fractional decay rate). From $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$, at $t = T_{1/2}$, $N = N_0/2$: $\tfrac12 = e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}}$, so $\ln2 = \lambda T_{1/2}$ and
A radioactive sample of mass $80\ \text{g}$ has half-life $4$ days. How much remains after $12$ days? Model answer: $12/4 = 3$ half-lives, so $N = 80\times\left(\tfrac12\right)^{3} = 10\ \text{g}$.

Calculate the binding energy and the binding energy per nucleon of $^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ ($m_p = 1.007825\ \text{u}$ for hydrogen atom, $m_n = 1.008665\ \text{u}$, $m_{He} = 4.002603\ \text{u}$, $1\ \text{u} = 931.5\ \text Model answer: Mass of constituents: $2(1.007825) + 2(1.008665) = 2.015650 + 2.017330 = 4.032980\ \text{u}$. Mass defect $= 4.032980 - 4.002603 = 0.030377\ \text{u}$. $B = 0.030377\times931.5 = 28.3\ \text{MeV}$; per nucleon $= 28.3/4 = 7.07\ \text{MeV}$.

State the law of radioactive decay and derive $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$. Draw the decay curve and mark $T_{1/2}$. Model answer: (a) Law: the rate of decay of a radioactive sample is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present. $-\dfrac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N$. Separating variables, $\dfrac{dN}{N} = -\lambda\,dt$. Integrating from $N_0$ at $t = 0$ to $N$ at $t$: $\ln\dfrac{N}{N_0} = -\lambda t$, so $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$. (b) (Graph: an

A body of mass $4\ \text{kg}$ moving at $6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ collides inelastically with a $2\ \text{kg}$ body at rest and they move together. Find the common velocity and the loss of kinetic energy. Model answer: $4\times6 = 6v$, $v = 4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Initial $K = \tfrac12(4)(36) = 72\ \text{J}$; final $K = \tfrac12(6)(16) = 48\ \text{J}$; loss $= 24\ \text{J}$.

Find the equivalent resistance of $4\ \Omega$ and $12\ \Omega$ in parallel, and the current from a $6\ \text{V}$ source through it. Model answer: $R = \dfrac{4\times12}{16} = 3\ \Omega$; $I = 6/3 = 2\ \text{A}$.

Find the temperature rise of $0.2\ \text{kg}$ of water when it absorbs $4200\ \text{J}$ of heat ($c = 4200\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$). Model answer: $\Delta\theta = \dfrac{Q}{mc} = \dfrac{4200}{0.2\times4200} = 5\ \text{K}$.

State Snell's law and find the refractive index if the angle of incidence is $45^{\circ}$ and of refraction $30^{\circ}$. Model answer: The ratio $\sin i/\sin r$ is constant for a given pair of media, and the incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in one plane. $n = \dfrac{\sin45^{\circ}}{\sin30^{\circ}} = \dfrac{0.7071}{0.5} = 1.41$.

Derive the work–energy theorem for a constant force and use it to find the stopping distance of a $1000\ \text{kg}$ car moving at $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ when a constant braking force of $5000\ \text{N}$ is applied. Model answer: For a constant force $F$ producing acceleration $a$ over displacement $s$: $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as$ with $a = F/m$ gives $Fs = \tfrac12mv^{2} - \tfrac12mu^{2}$: the work done by the net force equals the change in kinetic energy. Braking: $-5000\,s = 0 - \tfrac12(1000)(400) = -2.0\times10^{5}$, so $s = 40\ \text{m}$.

Define the principal focus of a convex lens, derive the thin-lens formula and find $f$ if an object at $40\ \text{cm}$ gives a real image at $24\ \text{cm}$. Model answer: The principal focus is the point on the axis at which rays parallel to the axis converge after refraction. Derivation: for an object $AB$ at $u$, ray $AO$ through the optical centre is undeviated; the ray parallel to the axis refracts through $F$. From similar triangles $ABO \sim A'B'O$: $\dfrac{h_o}{h_i} = \dfrac{u}{v

concepts.t: A $60\ \text{kg}$ person stands on a lift accelerating upward at $2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. Find the apparent weight ($g = 10$). Model answer: $R - mg = ma$, so $R = m(g + a) = 60\times12 = 720\ \text{N}$ (apparent weight, compared with $600\ \text{N}$ at rest).

concepts.u: Physics: Model Question Sets and Predicted Questions
concepts.t: Find the equivalent resistance between the ends when $2\ \Omega$ is in series with the parallel pair $3\ \Omega$ and $6\ \Omega$. Model answer: Parallel: $\dfrac{3\times6}{9} = 2\ \Omega$; total $2 + 2 = 4\ \Omega$.

concepts.t: A sample has $5\ \text{g}$ left after $12$ days from $40\ \text{g}$. Find its half-life. Model answer: $40/5 = 8 = 2^{3}$, so $3T_{1/2} = 12$ days and $T_{1/2} = 4$ days.

concepts.t: Derive the expression for the energy stored in a charged capacitor and find the energy released when a $20\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor charged to $50\ \text{V}$ is discharged. Model answer: Charging from $q$ to $q + dq$ against the p.d. $V = q/C$ needs $dW = \dfrac{q}{C}\,dq$. Total work $W = \int_0^Q\dfrac{q}{C}\,dq = \dfrac{Q^{2}}{2C} = \tfrac12CV^{2}$, stored as electric field energy. $U = \tfrac12(20\times10^{-6})(50)^{2} = 0.025\ \text{J}$, which is released as heat or light on discharge.

Model answer: A ray parallel to the axis strikes the mirror at $D$; the radius $CD$ is the normal, so the angle of incidence and reflection are equal, $\theta$. What is an antiparticle? Describe pair production and annihilation, giving the threshold energy for electron–positron pair production. Model answer: Outline: an antiparticle has the same mass and spin as its particle but opposite charge and opposite quantum numbers (§26.1). In pair production a photon passing close to a nucleus turns into a particle–antiparticle pair; for $e^{-}e^{+}$ the photon must carry at least $2m_ec^{2} = 1.02\ \text{MeV}$, and the nearby nuc

Distinguish between baryons and mesons, and show that the quark contents $uud$ and $u\bar{d}$ give the correct charges of the proton and the $\pi^{+}$. Model answer: Outline: baryons are three quarks with baryon number $+1$; mesons are a quark and an antiquark with baryon number $0$, and all mesons are unstable. Charges: $uud = \frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{3} = +1$ for the proton; $u\bar{d} = \frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{3} = +1$ for the $\pi^{+}$.

Why was the neutrino proposed, and why is it so difficult to detect? What does neutrino oscillation tell us about its mass? Model answer: Outline: beta-decay electrons emerge with a continuous energy spectrum, so Pauli (1930) proposed an unseen neutral particle carrying off the missing energy and momentum. The neutrino is chargeless and interacts only weakly, so its chance of interacting in a detector is minute. Oscillation between flavours is possible o

What is dark matter? Give two pieces of observational evidence for it. Model answer: Outline: dark matter is matter that has mass and therefore gravitates, but neither emits nor absorbs light, so it is seen only through its gravity (§26.2). Evidence: (i) flat galactic rotation curves — outer stars orbit far faster than the visible mass allows, requiring $M(r) \propto r$ out to large radii; (ii) gravita

Show that a star orbiting at radius $r$ inside a galaxy of enclosed mass $M(r)$ has speed $v = \sqrt{GM(r)/r}$, and explain why a flat rotation curve requires $M(r) \propto r$. Model answer: Gravity supplies the centripetal force, $GM(r)m/r^{2} = mv^{2}/r$. Cancelling $m$ and multiplying by $r$ gives $v^{2} = GM(r)/r$, so $v = \sqrt{GM(r)/r}$. If $v$ is constant then $M(r) = v^{2}r/G$, which is proportional to $r$: mass keeps accumulating outside the visible disc.

A gravitational wave of strain $1.0\times10^{-21}$ crosses a detector whose arms are $4.0\ \text{km}$ long. Calculate the change in length of one arm. Model answer: $\Delta L = hL = 1.0\times10^{-21}\times4.0\times10^{3} = 4.0\times10^{-18}\ \text{m}$, roughly one four-hundredth of a proton diameter.

Model answer: (a) A black hole is a region whose escape velocity exceeds the speed of light, so no radiation can leave it; its boundary at $r = R_s$ is the event horizon. Define parenchyma tissue and explain its structure and function. Model answer: Definition [1]. Parenchyma is a living, simple permanent tissue made of thin-walled cells that can still divide. Structure [2]. The cells are round, oval or polygonal; the primary wall is thin cellulose; there is a large central vacuole, a peripheral nucleus and usually small intercellular spaces. Define vascular bundle. What type of vascular bundle is present in a monocot root? Mention any two functions of a vascular bundle. Model answer: Definition [1]. A vascular bundle is a strand of conducting tissue made up of xylem and phloem (with or without cambium) that runs through the plant body. Wall material — cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin (collenchyma) versus lignin (sclerenchyma). Thickening — uneven, at corners or on particular walls, versus uniform and heavy with a narrow lumen. Explain the nature of the carbon–metal bond and use it to account for the reactivity order RLi > RMgX > R₂Cd. Model answer: Carbon (χ = 2.55) is more electronegative than the metals, so the bonding pair lies nearer carbon: Cδ⁻–Mδ⁺. Compare mechanical and chemical pulping under yield, strength, colour stability and use. Model answer: See the table in §20.3: mechanical 90–95 % yield, weak short fibres, yellows in light, used for newsprint; chemical 45–55 % yield, strong fibres, colour-stable, used for printing, writing and packaging paper.

Describe the Kraft process, giving the composition of white liquor, the cooking conditions and the equations of chemical recovery. Model answer: Chips are cooked with white liquor (NaOH + Na₂S) at about 170 °C and 7–8 atm for 2–4 hours; lignin dissolves, leaving cellulose. Recovery: Na₂SO₄ + 2C → Na₂S + 2CO₂↑ in the furnace; Na₂CO₃ + Ca(OH)₂ → 2NaOH + CaCO₃↓ in the causticiser; CaCO₃ --Δ--> CaO + CO₂↑ and CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ in the lime kiln.

What is the purpose of (i) bleaching, (ii) beating, (iii) sizing and (iv) loading? Name one chemical used in each. Model answer: (i) Bleaching removes residual lignin and whitens the pulp — ClO₂ or H₂O₂. (ii) Beating frays and swells the fibres so they bond — mechanical, no chemical. (iii) Sizing makes the sheet resist ink spread — rosin with alum, Al₂(SO₄)₃. (iv) Loading fills the gaps for opacity and smoothness — china clay, CaCO₃ or TiO₂.

List six properties by which the quality of paper is judged and explain why acid-free paper lasts longer. Model answer: Grammage, caliper, brightness, opacity, strength (tensile, burst, tear), sizing or Cobb value, ash content, pH, smoothness. Acid-free paper (pH 7–9) is not slowly hydrolysed at its glycosidic links, so the cellulose chains keep their length and the sheet does not become brown and brittle.

(Model) Model answer: The central idea is that knowledge and wisdom are different, that our age has gained enormously in knowledge without a corresponding increase in wisdom, and that knowledge may become harmful unless it is combined with wisdom, which can and should be taught.

How can wisdom be taught? Give examples. (Model) Model answer: Russell says it can be taught "in some degree", by giving moral teaching a larger intellectual element: in the course of teaching facts, teachers can point out the disastrous results of hatred and narrow-mindedness. For example, when teaching atomic physics they can show how the atom has been used for destruction; by a

Why does Russell say that Hegel lacked wisdom? Model answer: Hegel's philosophy of history was comprehensive in time, but its chief lesson was that from 400 AD Germany had been the most important nation and the standard-bearer of progress. His national pride distorted the facts, so he lacked the awareness of the ends of human life and the freedom from prejudice that wisdom needs

What point does Russell make through Mr A and Mr B? Model answer: Two men who hate each other and are ruined by their hatred each give an equally one-sided list of the other's vices, partly true and partly false. By showing each that the other says the same, a wise person can make both see that the other has "only the normal share of human wickedness" and that their enmity harms both

What does Russell mean by "the tyranny of the here and now"? Model answer: It means the natural self-centredness of our senses and feelings, which tie us to our own bodies, needs and moment. An infant knows only its own hunger. Wisdom is freedom from this as far as possible, by understanding and caring about things remote in time and space.

Why does Russell refuse to say that it is right to hate those who do harm? Model answer: Because hatred makes the hater as harmful as the enemy and is unlikely to persuade anyone to give up evil ways. "Hatred of evil is itself a kind of bondage to evil." The way out is understanding, though he does not advocate non-resistance: resistance should use the smallest force compatible with preserving what is good

Discuss Russell's view of wisdom and the factors that contribute to it. (Model) Model answer: Russell begins from the fact that our age far surpasses earlier ages in knowledge, without a corresponding increase in wisdom. He defines wisdom through its factors. The first is a sense of proportion, the capacity to take account of all the important factors in a problem and give each its due weight; specialists often

He holds that hatred of evil is "a kind of bondage to e

Model answer: According to Russell, wisdom is more necessary than ever because the power of knowledge has grown enormously. Nuclear weapons, unknown to

What are the universal human abilities according to Harari? Model answer: According to Harari, the universal human abilities are morality, art, spirituality and creativity. They are "embedded in our DNA", he says, and they began in Stone Age Africa, long before any present-day nation or religion.

The essayist calls on readers around the world to "puncture the hot-air balloons inflated by their own tribes". What do you think is the reason behind this? (Model) Model answer: History is a contested issue first because it gives a group its identity and pride. Harari's catalogue shows that every group wants to be the origin of civilisation, because being first seems to give a right to respect and leadership. Second, history is used as a political tool: governments use the past to justify thei

Humility means not thinking oneself more important than one is, and the whole essay is about its opposite, pride in one's group, which Harari calls "crass egotism". concepts.u: Human Rights and the Age of Inequality
concepts.t: Who is Samuel Moyn, and what is he best known for? Model answer: Samuel Moyn is an American professor of law and history at Yale University. He is known for critical studies of the history of human rights, such as The Last Utopia (2010) and Not Enough (2018).

concepts.u: Human Rights and the Age of Inequality
concepts.t: What is the difference between status equality and distributive equality? Model answer: Status equality means everyone has the same standing and basic rights as a person, as in Article 1 of the UDHR. Distributive equality concerns how wealth is shared, including any limit on the gap between rich and poor. The UDHR has the first but not the second.

concepts.u: Human Rights and the Age of Inequality
concepts.t: What does Moyn mean by a "floor of protection" and a "ceiling on inequality"? Model answer: A floor of protection is a minimum standard of living, such as food, health care and schooling, that everyone must be raised to. A ceiling on inequality is a limit on how far the richest can rise above the rest. Human rights offer the floor but not the ceiling.

concepts.u: Human Rights and the Age of Inequality
concepts.t: Why does Moyn call the UDHR's first article "a revolutionary act"? Model answer: Because in a world "devastated by the evils of racism and genocide", proclaiming that every human being is born free and equal in dignity and rights was a bold break with the ideas that had justified those evils, even though it said nothing about how wealth should be shared.

concepts.u: Human Rights and the Age of Inequality
concepts.t: What was Roosevelt's "highest promise" in his 1944 speech, according to Moyn? Model answer: It was not just a floor of protection for the masses but the end of "special privilege for the few", a ceiling on inequality, which Moyn says people overlook because they remember only "freedom from want".

concepts.u: Human Rights and the Age of Inequality
concepts.t: What irony does Moyn find in the 1974 Nobel Prize in economics? Model answer: Myrdal, who hoped to spread welfare worldwide, and Hayek, the champion of free markets, shared the prize; but Moyn says "where one of them was forgotten, the other saw his fondest wishes come true": market fundamentalism won.

concepts.u: Human Rights and the Age of Inequality
concepts.t: What does the hammer-and-nail image tell us about the human rights movement? Model answer: Human rights have become so successful that people use them as the tool for every problem, like a man who has only a hammer and treats everything like a nail. The image warns that rights are not suited to reduce inequality.

concepts.u: Human Rights and the Age of Inequality
concepts.t: Why does Moyn say a supplement, not a substitute, is needed? Model answer: Because human rights law works well against repression and violence and Moyn does not want to throw that away; what is missing is a separate political force for redistribution that can stand beside rights. So a supplement is needed, not a replacement.

concepts.u: Human Rights and the Age of Inequality
concepts.t: Explain Moyn's argument that human rights are "not equipped to challenge global inequalities". Model answer: Moyn's claim is that human rights law and movements aim at a floor, not a ceiling. The UDHR announced status equality ("born free and equal in dignity and rights"), but it does not mention distributive equality, any limit on the wealth gap between rich and poor. As Moyn puts it, one could "imagine one man owning everyt

concepts.u: Human Rights and the Age of Inequality
concepts.t: How does Moyn trace the history of human rights in relation to political economy? Model answer: Moyn uses two stages. In the first, the heroic age of national welfare states (1940s-1970s), human rights were a modest, optional synonym for the welfare consensus reached "after depression and war". Roosevelt's 1944 call for a "second bill of rights" promised "freedom from want" and, more importantly, the end of "spec

concepts.u: Human Rights and the Age of Inequality
concepts.t: Do you agree with Moyn that human rights need a supplement rather than a substitute? Give reasons with reference to Nepal. Model answer: Moyn says human rights cannot close the wealth gap, so they need a supplement: a politics of redistribution with the power to frighten the privileged. I agree. Human rights are valuable: they protect people from torture, censorship and arbitrary arrest, and many Nepalis rely on the rights in the 2015 Constitution and o

concepts.u: Human Rights and the Age of Inequality
concepts.t: Write a paragraph on how the gap between rich and poor can be narrowed in your country. Model answer: Suggest progressive taxes, well-funded public schools and health posts in remote districts, land and housing programmes, employment and skills training, transparent governance, and strong civic movements. End with Moyn's insight that change needs political pressure, not just good laws.

Why has the Earnest Young Woman come to the Famous Actress? Model answer: She believes her husband, the lawyer Alfred, has fallen in love with the actress, and she has come to beg the actress to "give me back my husband".

How does the actress first answer the wife's plea? Model answer: The actress pretends to be bewildered. She says she cannot return a husband she has not got, and that she knows Alfred only as the lawyer who drew up her last contract and whom she has seen backstage.

What evidence of the affair does the wife produce? Model answer: She says he sends flowers to the actress's dressing room twice a week (she learned it at the florist's), she reads a letter found on his desk ("My darling... Ten thousand kisses. Alfred"), and she has a lock of the actress's hair found in his drawer.

What does the actress say is "one of the oldest expedients in the world"? Model answer: Inventing a love affair with an actress to make a wife or sweetheart jealous and win back her affection. The actress says authors, composers, scene designers, lawyers, orchestra leaders and managers have all used it.

How does the actress explain the lock of hair? Model answer: She says men bribe her hairdresser to steal a lock, so Alfred's possession of it is part of his plan to make his wife jealous, not proof of a love affair.

What advice does the actress give the wife before she leaves? Model answer: She advises the wife not to be taken in a second time, no matter what letters, handkerchiefs, photographs or flowers she finds in his pockets, and promises not to tell Alfred about the visit.

What do the last words of the play reveal? Model answer: The actress calls out, "All right, Alfred. You can come in now. She has gone." They reveal that the husband has been hiding in her boudoir all the time, so the wife's suspicion was true and the actress has deceived her.

Why does the author call the characters "Famous Actress" and "Earnest Young Woman"? Model answer: They are types, not individuals: a woman of the theatre who lives by acting, and an ordinary, sincere woman. The labels highlight the contrast that drives the play: pretending versus plain dealing.

Discuss "A Matter of Husbands" as a comedy of deception. Model answer: The play is a comedy because it is built on deception that we enjoy watching. The wife comes to claim her husband and the actress denies any knowledge. Then the actress changes the ground: she turns each of the wife's proofs into a sign of something harmless. The wife leaves relieved; only in the last line, when the ac

Describe how the Famous Actress persuades the Earnest Young Woman that her husband is innocent. Model answer: The actress works in five steps. First she denies everything calmly, so the wife's certainty weakens. Second, she asks whether the couple have been getting on badly of late, whether they were once affectionate and whether the wife has grown cold; the wife's "Yes" to each supplies the premise of the actress's theory. Th

Discuss the use of irony and stage directions in the play. Model answer: Irony is the play's main method. Verbal irony: the actress says she is "neither better nor worse than any other girl in the theater" while deceiving a wife. Situational irony: the wife, who came to fight her rival, leaves grateful to her. Dramatic irony: the audience gradually suspects what the wife does not; and in th

Write a paragraph describing your favourite actor or actress. Model answer: Give the name; say what he or she is famous for, three qualities of the acting (voice, emotion, range) and two or three works; end with why he or she inspires you. Use present tense and concrete examples.
Where and when is the play set? Model answer: The play is set in the dining-room of Durand's pension near Lake Léman in French Switzerland in the 1880s, on a morning when the house is bankrupt.

Why does Adèle complain when Pierre comes back from the baker? Model answer: Because Pierre brings no bread but three unpaid bills. The baker will send no more until he is paid and the butcher and grocer have also sent bills. She sees that the family's credit is finished.

Why does Antonio ask Durand whether he was born in Switzerland? Model answer: Antonio seems to have guessed that Durand may not be Swiss by birth. Durand answers "uncertainly" that he was, and later Thérèse and Durand himself reveal that he was born in France.

What does Durand do after seeing Antonio kiss Thérèse? Model answer: He lifts his stick against Antonio and tells him to choose his weapon; when Antonio leaves, Durand throws a gold piece after him, breaks his stick in two and says, "He who cannot kill must die."

What do the daughters take from Durand, and what does Thérèse give back at the end? Model answer: They take his glass of milk and his matches. At the end Thérèse says, "Here are your matches, papa--and there's your milk" and runs into his arms: the only things she has to give.

What is the meaning of the candle that Durand counts with Adèle? Model answer: The packet should hold six candles but has five; the sixth has been placed "very high up and very near" something that will burn, and will be burned out in "five minutes or so". It is the fuse that will start the fire.

What does Durand ask Adèle to do for her sisters? Model answer: He asks her to take motherly care of Thérèse and see her married soon, to find a place as a teacher for Annette, to manage the money carefully, to keep the family papers, never to tell her sisters what he has done and never to speak ill of their mother.

How does the play end? Model answer: Smoke comes through the ceiling and bells ring outside. Adèle sees that Durand has taken poison. He asks whether she has the insurance papers and begins to say "Tell Thérèse--and Annette--" when his head falls on the table. The curtain falls.

Describe Monsieur Durand as a tragic hero. Model answer: A tragic hero is a central figure whom we pity because he suffers more than he deserves, and whose fall comes from character and circumstance. Durand is such a figure in a modern key. He is a good man: patient, honourable and tender. He buys candles for a dead child, says that he once got up at night to cover his daugh

How does Strindberg use symbols and foreshadowing to prepare for the ending? Model answer: The play prepares the ending through clues that seem ordinary until the last minutes. Foreshadowing: on the first page Durand tells Adèle to put out the fire in the stove and Adèle asks whether the fire insurance is paid; Durand wishes everything would "crash at once"; the wind is "going to blow soon"; a clanging is he

Is Durand's decision to kill himself justified? Discuss with reference to the play. Model answer: The play does not condemn or approve; it asks us to understand. In favour: Durand is bankrupt, unable to borrow "a sou", despised by his children and worn out by years of humiliation; his daughters face homelessness; death will bring them money, and he arranges their future carefully, with marriages and a teaching post

Write a short essay on "The Sacrifices of Parents". Model answer: Open with the idea that parents give time, food and dreams before being asked. Give two examples from life and one from the play (Durand's candle, milk, death). Discuss how children can thank them. End with a short promise.

Do you think a family's poverty can destroy love? Discuss with examples. Model answer: Take a side. Poverty can strain love, as the Durand daughters' cruelty shows, but it can also reveal it: Thérèse's last gift of matches and milk. Mention support, communication and honesty as the things that protect a family.
Who is Bhimnidhi Tiwari? Model answer: Bhimnidhi Tiwari (1911-1973) was a Nepali poet, story-writer and dramatist, and a social reformer who founded the Nepal Natak Sangh to promote Nepali plays.
What is the name of the bull and who owns it? Model answer: The bull is called Male. It belongs to King Ranabahadur Shah, who is very fond of bulls.

Why are Laxminarayan, Jitman and Gore afraid of the king? Model answer: Because the king's bull has died in their care, and the king is known to punish people severely. They fear being beheaded or shaved as a punishment, though the bull died of natural causes or rich food.

What excuse does Laxminarayan give the king for moving the bull? Model answer: He says the bull is ill, will not eat, move or speak, and needs a change of climate; he asks to take it to the hills. This is a lie to hide that the bull is already dead.
What does Laxminarayan tell the cowherds to do before the king arrives? Model answer: He tells them to massage the bull's back feet and fan it as if it were alive, and not to reveal that it is dead.

What does the word "chakari" mean? Model answer: Chakari is serving and flattering a person of higher rank to win his favour; it also means pleading before such a person by showing one's poverty or distress.

Name two things that show the bull is treated better than the cowherds. Model answer: The bull has a mattress, quilt and mosquito net and is fed fine rice and lentil soup, while the cowherds sleep on straw in winter and live in fear.

Discuss "The Bull" as a satire on the feudal system. Model answer: A satire exposes the faults of people or society through humour. "The Bull" exposes the feudal system, in which a king and lords hold all power. The first fault is the dehumanisation of ordinary people: the king's bull has a mattress, quilt and mosquito net, while the cowherds sleep on straw; the men's lives are at ris

How does Laxminarayan save himself and the cowherds? What does this tell us about him? Model answer: Laxminarayan saves himself and the cowherds by controlling what the king knows. When Jitman and Gore bring the news, he keeps it secret and goes to the palace. There he says the bull is ill and praises its beauty and courage, and suggests a change of climate in the hills, so that any death could happen out of sight. Wh

Discuss the use of irony and humour in the play. Model answer: Irony is the source of the humour. Dramatic irony: the audience knows from the start that the bull is dead and watches Laxminarayan lie to a king who does not know. Situational irony: men who did nothing wrong are terrified, and in the end they are rewarded for lying; a king who could have punished them pays them. Verb

Write a paragraph on "The Role of Satire in Society". Model answer: Define satire; say it uses humour and exaggeration to expose faults; give examples (newspaper cartoons, comic plays, "The Bull"); explain how laughter can change attitudes more than lecture; end by noting that satire must be fair and aim at injustice, not individuals.
The programme starts at ten, isn't it? Model answer: The programme starts at ten, doesn't it? — the subject is a thing, so it, not isn't it.
Where he has gone since morning? Model answer: Where has he gone since morning? — a direct question inverts the operator and the subject.
Who did break this window? Model answer: Who broke this window? — who is the subject here, so no did.
Can you tell me when does the library open? Model answer: Can you tell me when the library opens? — an embedded question keeps statement order.
Does your father works in a bank? Model answer: Does your father work in a bank? — after does, the base form.
Why you did not attend the meeting? Model answer: Why didn't you attend the meeting? — the operator must come before the subject.
Where is the ticket counter? — Rewrite beginning Could you tell me … Model answer: Could you tell me where the ticket counter is? — the embedded clause returns to statement order.
Does he can come with us tomorrow? Model answer: Can he come with us tomorrow? — modals form questions without do.
The teacher gave us many informations about the scholarship. Model answer: … gave us much information about the scholarship. — information is uncountable.
The most of the villagers depend on farming. Model answer: Most of the villagers depend on farming. — no the before most of.
The list of selected candidates have been published. Model answer: The list of selected candidates has been published. — the subject is the list.
The committee have announced their decision unanimously. Model answer: The committee has announced its decision unanimously. — acting as one body, and unanimously shows it.

The teachers and the principal were present. — Rewrite beginning Not only the teachers but also … Model answer: Not only the teachers but also the principal was present. — the proximity rule makes the verb singular.
The mangoes of Nepal are sweeter than India. Model answer: The mangoes of Nepal are sweeter than those of India. — compare mangoes with mangoes.
The guide said, "The Himalayas lie to the north of Nepal." Model answer: The guide said that the Himalayas lie to the north of Nepal. — a permanent geographical fact does not shift.
The teacher said to the boys, "Why are you making noise?" Model answer: The teacher asked the boys why they were making noise. — wh-word kept, statement order, no question mark.
The teacher said that the earth moved round the sun. Model answer: The teacher said that the earth moves round the sun. — a universal truth stays in the present.
The officer ordered the peon to bring the file at once. Model answer: The officer said to the peon, "Bring the file at once." — the infinitive becomes an imperative.
If I (be) you, I would consult a doctor. Model answer: were — type 2; were is used for all persons in the unreal past.

If she had taken the medicine, she (recover) by now. Model answer: would have recovered — type 3; the condition and the result are both past and unfulfilled. (would be well by now would be the mixed form.)
If it will rain, the programme will be cancelled. Model answer: If it rains, the programme will be cancelled. — no will in the if-clause.
If I would have known, I would have told you. Model answer: If I had known, I would have told you. — type 3 uses the past perfect.
If I was a bird, I would fly over the Himalayas. Model answer: If I were a bird, I would fly over the Himalayas. — unreal were.
If had he apologised, she would have forgiven him. Model answer: Had he apologised, she would have forgiven him. — with inversion, if is deleted.
If you do not water the plants, they will die. — Use unless. Model answer: Unless you water the plants, they will die. — the negative disappears with unless.
If she had not helped me, I would have been in trouble. — Begin: But for … Model answer: But for her help, I would have been in trouble. — but for is followed by a noun phrase.
If I were rich, I would build a school in my village. — Begin: Were … Model answer: Were I rich, I would build a school in my village. — if is deleted and were moves in front of the subject.
The postman delivers the letters every morning. Model answer: The letters are delivered (by the postman) every morning. — simple present: are + V3.
The committee will announce the results tomorrow. Model answer: The results will be announced by the committee tomorrow. — future: will be + V3.
The teacher gave Sita a prize. Model answer: Sita was given a prize by the teacher. (or A prize was given to Sita by the teacher.) — the person-first passive is preferred.
The villagers are looking after the orphans. Model answer: The orphans are being looked after by the villagers. — the preposition after stays with the verb.
A new hospital is going to be built here. Model answer: They are going to build a new hospital here. — supply a general subject when no agent is given.
Let the lights be switched off. Model answer: Switch off the lights. — Let … be + V3 is the passive of an imperative.
The letter has written by the secretary. Model answer: The letter has been written by the secretary. — the passive needs been.
The problem was discussed about for two hours. Model answer: The problem was discussed for two hours. — discuss takes no about.
The glass was broke by the cat. Model answer: The glass was broken by the cat. — past participle, not past tense.
The teacher told us that the sun (rise) in the east. Model answer: rises — a universal truth does not shift after a past reporting verb.
The pen is missing. I bought it yesterday. — Join with a defining clause. Model answer: The pen (that) I bought yesterday is missing. — the pronoun is the object, so it may be dropped.
The girl who is sitting near the window is my cousin. — Reduce the relative clause. Model answer: The girl sitting near the window is my cousin. — who is is deleted and the -ing form remains.

Define moment of inertia. Derive the moment of inertia of a uniform rod about an axis through one end and perpendicular to its length. Model answer: (a) The moment of inertia of a body about an axis is the sum $\sum mr^{2}$ of the products of the mass of each particle and the square of its perpendicular distance from the axis. It is the rotational analogue of mass: it measures the body's resistance to a change in its rotation. Unit: $\text{kg m}^{2}$.

Model answer: (a) The radius of gyration $k$ is the distance from the axis at which the whole mass of the body could be concentrated without changing its moment of inertia: $I = Mk^{2}$, so $k = \sqrt{I/M}$.
