The speed at A Model answer: (a) Bernoulli's principle: for the steady, non-viscous, incompressible flow of a fluid, the sum of the pressure, the kinetic energy per unit volume and the potential energy per unit volume is constant along a streamline: where the speed is high, the pressure is low.

State Stokes' law. Derive the expression for the terminal velocity of a small sphere falling through a viscous fluid. Model answer: (a) The viscous drag on a small sphere of radius $r$ moving at speed $v$ in a fluid of viscosity $\eta$ is $F = 6\pi\eta rv$.

Derive Bernoulli's equation and state the assumptions made. Explain the working of a Venturi meter and derive the speed of flow from the two pressures. Model answer: (a) See short answer 5(a) for the derivation from the work–energy theorem,

Derive the expression for the rise of a liquid in a capillary tube. Give two applications of capillarity. Model answer: (a) Water of surface tension $T$ rises in a tube of radius $r$ with contact angle $\theta$. The surface tension acts along the line of contact of length $2\pi r$, at angle $\theta$ to the wall; the vertical component of the pull is

Define surface tension and surface energy and show that they are numerically equal. Model answer: Outline: $T = F/L$; surface energy $= W/\Delta A$. For a film on a frame of width $l$ pulled out a distance $x$, $W = 2Tl\,x = T(2lx) = T\Delta A$, so $1\ \text{N m}^{-1} = 1\ \text{J m}^{-2}$.

A capillary tube of internal radius $0.5\ \text{mm}$ is dipped vertically in water of surface tension $0.072\ \text{N m}^{-1}$. Calculate the rise. ($\theta = 0^{\circ}$, $\rho = 1000\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$) Model answer: $h = \dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{r\rho g} = \dfrac{2(0.072)}{(5\times10^{-4})(1000)(9.8)} = \dfrac{0.144}{4.9} = 0.0294\ \text{m} = 2.94\ \text{cm}$.

State Stokes' law and derive the terminal velocity of a sphere in a viscous liquid. Hence find the terminal velocity of an air bubble of radius $1\ \text{mm}$ rising through a liquid of density $1200\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$ a Model answer: For a rising bubble the upthrust exceeds the weight; taking the air density as negligible, $v_t = \dfrac{2r^{2}\sigma g}{9\eta} = \dfrac{2(10^{-3})^{2}(1200)(9.8)}{9(0.5)} = 5.23\times10^{-3}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, about $5.2\ \text{mm s}^{-1}$ upwards.

Define angle of contact and explain why water wets glass but mercury does not. Derive an expression for the rise of a liquid in a capillary tube and calculate the rise of water in a tube of internal radius $0.1\ \text{mm Model answer: (b) $h = \dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{r\rho g} = \dfrac{2(0.072)}{(10^{-4})(1000)(9.8)} = \dfrac{0.144}{0.98} = 0.147\ \text{m} = 14.7\ \text{cm}$.

State Bernoulli's principle and derive Bernoulli's equation for the streamline flow of an ideal liquid. A tank on the ground holds water to a depth of $3\ \text{m}$. A small hole is made in its side $1.2\ \text{m}$ below Model answer: (b) $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2(9.8)(1.2)} = 4.85\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. The hole is $1.8\ \text{m}$ above the ground and the jet leaves horizontally, so $t = \sqrt{2(1.8)/9.8} = 0.606\ \text{s}$ and $x = vt = 2.94\ \text{m}$.

State the first law of thermodynamics. Derive $C_P-C_V = R$ for an ideal gas. Model answer: (a) The first law: the heat supplied to a system equals the increase in its internal energy plus the work done by the system: $Q = \Delta U + W$.

What is an indicator diagram? Show that the work done by a gas in a volume change is the area under its $p$–$V$ curve. Model answer: (a) An indicator diagram is a graph of pressure against volume ($p$–$V$ diagram) for a system or an engine cycle.

Explain how the first law expresses the conservation of energy. Write what the law reduces to in (i) an isothermal, (ii) an adiabatic, (iii) an isochoric and (iv) an isobaric process. Model answer: (a) Energy can be neither created nor destroyed. Heat $Q$ is energy supplied to the system; it either raises the internal (molecular) energy, $\Delta U$, or leaves the system as work, $W$ done on the surroundings. Nothing is lost, so the accounts balance: $Q = \Delta U+W$.

Define the two principal heat capacities of an ideal gas. Derive the relation between them. Model answer: (a) The molar heat capacity at constant volume, $C_V$, is the heat needed to raise the temperature of one mole by one kelvin with the volume held fixed; $C_P$ is the corresponding heat at constant pressure. Units: $\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$.

Describe the isothermal and adiabatic processes of an ideal gas and sketch both on one $p$–$V$ diagram. Derive the work done in an adiabatic expansion from $(P_1, V_1)$ to $(P_2, V_2)$. Model answer: (a) Isothermal: the temperature is fixed (slow change, good thermal contact with a reservoir); $PV = \text{constant}$ and $\Delta U = 0$. Adiabatic: no heat flows (rapid change or perfect insulation); $PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$ with $\gamma>1$, so the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isotherm through the same p

Define internal energy. State the first law of thermodynamics, write it in differential form, and explain the sign convention used for $Q$ and $W$. Model answer: Internal energy is the total kinetic plus potential energy of the molecules of a system, measured in its own frame; it is a state function. First law: $Q = \Delta U + W$, i.e. $dQ = dU + dW$. $Q$ is positive when heat is absorbed, $W$ is positive when the gas expands, $\Delta U$ is positive when the temperature rises.

Derive the relation $C_p - C_v = R$ for one mole of an ideal gas, and explain physically why $C_p$ must be greater than $C_v$. Model answer: See the derivation in §4.5. Physically, at constant volume all the heat goes into internal energy, whereas at constant pressure the gas must additionally do work $P\,dV = R\,dT$ against the surroundings, so more heat is needed for the same $dT$.

A gas expands at a constant pressure of $1.5\times10^{5}\ \text{Pa}$ from $2.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^{3}$ to $5.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^{3}$, absorbing $800\ \text{J}$ of heat. Calculate the work done and the change in Model answer: $W = P\Delta V = 1.5\times10^{5}\times(5.0-2.0)\times10^{-3} = 450\ \text{J}$. Then $\Delta U = Q - W = 800 - 450 = 350\ \text{J}$.

State the second law of thermodynamics. Does a refrigerator violate it? Explain. Model answer: (a) Kelvin–Planck statement: it is impossible to construct an engine, working in a cycle, whose sole effect is to take heat from a single reservoir and convert it completely into work. Clausius statement: heat cannot flow from a colder body to a hotter body by itself, with no other change.

Draw the $p$–$V$ diagram of a petrol engine and explain its working. Compare the efficiency of a petrol engine with that of a diesel engine in terms of compression ratio. Model answer: (a) The Otto cycle (figure below) models a petrol engine: $1\to2$ adiabatic compression of the fuel–air mixture from $V_1$ to $V_2$; $2\to3$ heating at constant volume when the spark ignites the mixture (heat $Q_1$ absorbed); $3\to4$ adiabatic expansion (the power stroke, which delivers the work); $4\to1$ cooling at co

Describe the four steps of the Carnot cycle. Write the efficiency and state why no engine can exceed it. Model answer: (a) Working substance: an ideal gas in a cylinder, between a source at $T_1$ and a sink at $T_2$. (i) Isothermal expansion at $T_1$: heat $Q_1$ absorbed from the source, work done by the gas. (ii) Adiabatic expansion: the gas cools from $T_1$ to $T_2$ with no heat exchange. (iii) Isothermal compression at $T_2$: heat $

Describe the Carnot cycle with a labelled $p$–$V$ diagram. Derive the efficiency $\eta = 1-T_2/T_1$. Model answer: (a) The cycle (figure below) consists of four reversible steps on an ideal gas: $A\to B$ isothermal expansion at $T_1$; $B\to C$ adiabatic expansion to $T_2$; $C\to D$ isothermal compression at $T_2$; $D\to A$ adiabatic compression to $T_1$.

Draw and explain the Otto and the Diesel cycles. Derive the efficiency of the Otto cycle. Model answer: (a) Otto cycle (petrol): two adiabats and two isochores, as explained in section 3.5 short answer 3(a). Diesel cycle: $1\to2$ adiabatic compression of air alone to a high ratio; $2\to3$ fuel injected and burns at constant pressure (heat $Q_1$ in, gas expands to $V_3$); $3\to4$ adiabatic expansion; $4\to1$ cooling at co

Explain how a refrigerator works, with a block diagram. A refrigerator removes $500\ \text{J}$ per cycle from the food compartment at $-3\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$ and rejects heat to a room at $27\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$. Find the Model answer: (a) A refrigerator is a heat engine run backwards. A compressor (driven by a motor, work $W$) compresses a refrigerant vapour, which gives up heat $Q_1$ in the condenser outside; the refrigerant then expands through a valve, cools and absorbs heat $Q_2$ in the evaporator inside the compartment; the cycle repeats. By en

A Carnot engine has an efficiency of $40\ \%$ when its sink is at $27\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$. Find the temperature of the source. To what temperature must the source be raised to obtain an efficiency of $50\ \%$, the sink be Model answer: $\eta = 1 - T_2/T_1$ gives $0.40 = 1 - 300/T_1$, so $T_1 = 300/0.60 = 500\ \text{K}$ ($227\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$). For $\eta = 0.50$, $T_1 = 300/0.50 = 600\ \text{K}$ ($327\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$) — a rise of $100\ \text{K}$.

Define the coefficient of performance of a refrigerator. A refrigerator with a COP of $5$ extracts $600\ \text{J}$ of heat per cycle from the cold chamber. Find the work done per cycle and the heat rejected to the surrou Model answer: COP is the ratio of the heat extracted from the cold body to the work supplied, $\beta = Q_2/W$. Here $W = Q_2/\beta = 600/5 = 120\ \text{J}$ and $Q_1 = Q_2 + W = 600 + 120 = 720\ \text{J}$.

Define a progressive wave and a stationary wave. Write the equation of a plane progressive wave and explain every symbol. Model answer: (a) A progressive wave is a disturbance that travels through a medium, transferring energy from one place to another without transferring the medium itself. A stationary (standing) wave is formed by the superposition of two identical progressive waves travelling in opposite directions; the pattern stays in place and no

Explain how a stationary wave is formed. Prove that the distance between two consecutive nodes is $\lambda/2$. Model answer: (a) A wave travelling along a string is reflected at the fixed end with a phase change of $\pi$. The incident and reflected waves, of the same frequency and amplitude, travel in opposite directions and superpose. At some points they always cancel (nodes); at others they always reinforce (antinodes). The pattern does no

State the principle of superposition. Two pulses of heights $+2\ \text{cm}$ and $+3\ \text{cm}$ travel towards each other on a string; describe what you see as they meet and after. Model answer: (a) Superposition: when two or more waves overlap, the resultant displacement at any point is the algebraic sum of the displacements that each wave would produce alone.

Derive the equation of a stationary wave formed on a string fixed at both ends. Find the positions of nodes and antinodes. Model answer: (a) Let the incident wave be $y_1 = A\sin(\omega t-kx)$. At the fixed end the reflected wave is $y_2 = -A\sin(\omega t+kx)$ for a reflection with a phase change of $\pi$ (taking the end at $x = 0$). Adding,

Derive the equation $y = A\sin(\omega t-kx)$ for a progressive wave. Find the phase difference between two particles $x_1$ and $x_2$ apart. Model answer: (a) A source at $x = 0$ vibrates as $y = A\sin\omega t$. The disturbance travels at speed $v$, so a point at distance $x$ copies the source motion a time $x/v$ later:

What is a progressive wave? Derive the expression $y = a\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}(vt - x)$ for a wave travelling along the positive $x$ direction. Model answer: See §6.2: the particle at $x$ repeats the motion of the origin after a delay $x/v$, so $y = a\sin\omega(t - x/v)$; substituting $\omega = 2\pi/T$ and $v = \lambda/T$ gives the required form.

A transverse wave is represented by $y = 0.03\sin(40\pi t - 0.2\pi x)$ in SI units. Find its amplitude, frequency, wavelength, speed and maximum particle velocity. Model answer: $a = 0.03\ \text{m}$; $\omega = 40\pi$, so $f = 20\ \text{Hz}$; $k = 0.2\pi$, so $\lambda = 2\pi/0.2\pi = 10\ \text{m}$; $v = \omega/k = 40\pi/0.2\pi = 200\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (check: $f\lambda = 20\times10$); $(v_p)_{\max} = a\omega = 0.03\times40\pi = 3.77\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

A stationary wave is given by $y = 5\sin(0.4\pi x)\cos(100\pi t)$, with $y$ and $x$ in centimetres. Find the wavelength, frequency, wave speed and the distance between a node and the next antinode. Model answer: $k = 0.4\pi\ \text{cm}^{-1}$, so $\lambda = 2\pi/0.4\pi = 5\ \text{cm}$; $\omega = 100\pi$, so $f = 50\ \text{Hz}$; $v = f\lambda = 50 \times 0.05 = 2.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$; node to next antinode $= \lambda/4 = 1.25\ \text{cm}$.

State Newton's formula for the speed of sound in air and its discrepancy with experiment. State Laplace's correction. Model answer: (a) Newton: sound passes through air so slowly that the compressions and rarefactions are isothermal, and the speed is

State Laplace's correction and write the corrected formula. Find the wavelength in air at $25\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$ of a note of $256\ \text{Hz}$, given that the speed at $0\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$ is $330\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Model answer: (a) Laplace's correction: the changes of pressure and volume in a sound wave are adiabatic, not isothermal, so in Newton's formula $P$ must be replaced by $\gamma P$ (because the adiabatic bulk modulus of an ideal gas is $\gamma P$):

How do temperature and pressure affect the speed of sound in a gas? How does humidity affect it? Model answer: (a) For an ideal gas $P/\rho = RT/M$, so $v = \sqrt{\gamma RT/M}\propto\sqrt{T}$: the speed rises with temperature, about $0.61\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ per $^{\circ}\text{C}$ near room temperature. At constant temperature a change of pressure has no effect, because $\rho\propto P$ and the ratio $P/\rho$ stays constant.

Write the expressions for the speed of a longitudinal wave in a solid and in a liquid. Find the speed in steel ($Y = 2.0\times10^{11}\ \text{Pa}$, $\rho = 7800\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$) and in water ($K = 2.2\times10^{9}\ \tex Model answer: (a) Solid: $v = \sqrt{Y/\rho}$, where $Y$ is Young's modulus. Liquid: $v = \sqrt{K/\rho}$, where $K$ is the bulk modulus. (A solid also carries transverse waves at $\sqrt{\eta/\rho}$, with $\eta$ the rigidity modulus.)

Derive the expression for the speed of a longitudinal pulse in a fluid in terms of its bulk modulus and density. Hence state Newton's formula and Laplace's correction. Model answer: (a) Let a piston in a long tube of fluid (cross-section $A$, density $\rho$, bulk modulus $B$) suddenly move with speed $u$ for a time $\Delta t$. A compression pulse travels ahead at speed $v$, so in $\Delta t$ it covers $v\Delta t$ of fluid, which has mass $\rho Av\Delta t$ and is brought from rest to speed $u$. The

Explain the effect of (i) temperature, (ii) pressure and (iii) humidity on the speed of sound. A bat emits a pulse and hears the echo from a wall $0.50\ \text{s}$ later at an air temperature of $20\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$ ($v Model answer: (a) (i) Temperature: $v\propto\sqrt{T}$, so heating air makes sound faster, by about $0.61\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ per degree. (ii) Pressure: no effect if $T$ is constant, because $P/\rho$ is constant. (iii) Humidity: moist air is less dense, so the speed is higher.

Derive Newton's formula for the velocity of sound in a gas and state the assumption on which it rests. Why does it fail? Model answer: Isothermal assumption, $PV=$ const, $P\,dV+V\,dP=0$, hence $B=P$ and $v=\sqrt{P/\rho}$. It gives 280 m s⁻¹ against a measured 332 m s⁻¹ — a 16 % error — because sound compressions are far too rapid, and air far too poor a conductor, for the heat to escape.

State and explain Laplace's correction. Show that it raises the calculated velocity in air at NTP from about 280 m s⁻¹ to about 331 m s⁻¹. (Take $P=1.013\times10^{5}\ \text{Pa}$, $\rho=1.293\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$, $\gamma=1 Model answer: Adiabatic: $PV^{\gamma}=$ const gives $B=\gamma P$, so $v=\sqrt{\gamma P/\rho}$. Numerically $\sqrt{1.013\times10^{5}/1.293}=280\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, and $280\times\sqrt{1.4}=280\times1.183=331\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

Show that the velocity of sound in air increases by about 0.61 m s⁻¹ for a rise of 1 °C, given that it is 332 m s⁻¹ at 0 °C. Model answer: $v_t=v_0(1+t/273)^{1/2}\approx v_0(1+t/546)$, so $v_t-v_0 = v_0 t/546 = (332/546)t = 0.61t$. For $t=1\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$ the increase is 0.61 m s⁻¹.

The velocity of sound in a certain liquid is 1500 m s⁻¹ and its density is 1200 kg m⁻³. Find the bulk modulus of the liquid. Model answer: $v=\sqrt{B/\rho}\Rightarrow B=\rho v^{2}=1200\times(1500)^{2} = 1200\times2.25\times10^{6} = 2.7\times10^{9}\ \text{Pa}$.

Explain why sound travels faster in solids than in liquids, and faster in liquids than in gases, even though solids are the densest of the three. Model answer: Speed is $\sqrt{E/\rho}$. Going gas → liquid → solid the density rises by a factor of roughly $10^{3}$ and then 8, but the elastic modulus rises by a far larger factor (about $10^{4}$ from air to water and about $10^{2}$ again from water to steel). Stiffness therefore wins over inertia.

Define harmonic and overtone. A string $0.80\ \text{m}$ long, under tension $64\ \text{N}$, has mass per unit length $4.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{kg m}^{-1}$: find the frequency of its first overtone. Model answer: (a) The lowest frequency of a vibrating system is the fundamental (first harmonic). Higher frequencies that are integer multiples of it are harmonics (second, third, …). An overtone is any mode above the fundamental: the first overtone is the second harmonic (for an open pipe or a string), the second overtone is the th

A flute $30\ \text{cm}$ long, open at both ends, sounds its first harmonic; find the frequency ($v = 330\ \text{m s}^{-1}$). Define harmonic in music. Model answer: (a) An open pipe has antinodes at both ends and $L = \lambda/2$ for the fundamental:

Describe the stationary waves in an open and in a closed organ pipe, drawing the first three modes of each. Derive the frequencies of the harmonics for both. Model answer: (a) Open pipe: both ends are antinodes of displacement (pressure nodes). The three simplest modes have $L = \lambda/2,\ \lambda,\ 3\lambda/2$ (figure below, left). Closed pipe: the closed end is a node, the open end an antinode; the modes have $L = \lambda/4,\ 3\lambda/4,\ 5\lambda/4$ (figure below, right).

Derive $f_n = \dfrac{n}{2L}\sqrt{T/\mu}$ for a string fixed at both ends. A guitar string of length $1.5\ \text{m}$ is made of steel of density $7800\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$ and Young's modulus $2\times10^{11}\ \text{N m}^{-2 Model answer: (a) A transverse wave on a string travels at $v = \sqrt{T/\mu}$. For a string fixed at both ends of length $L$, both ends are nodes, so the stationary wave must fit an integral number of half-wavelengths: $L = n\lambda_n/2$, $\lambda_n = 2L/n$. Then

State the laws of vibration of a fixed string and describe the sonometer experiment that verifies the law of length. Two wires of the same material, radii in the ratio $1:2$, are stretched with equal tension and have equ Model answer: (a) The laws are stated in short answer 5(a). Sonometer experiment: a wire is stretched over two bridges on a wooden box and kept under a fixed tension by a hanging load. A tuning fork of known frequency is sounded and a light paper rider is placed on the wire; the movable bridge is adjusted until the rider is thrown o

Show that a closed organ pipe produces only odd harmonics while an open pipe of the same length produces all harmonics, and hence compare their fundamental frequencies. Model answer: Closed: node at one end, antinode at the other, so $L = (2n-1)\lambda/4$ and $f_n = (2n-1)v/4L$ — odd harmonics. Open: antinodes at both ends, so $L = n\lambda/2$ and $f_n = nv/2L$ — all harmonics. For the same $L$, $f_1(\text{open}) = 2f_1(\text{closed})$.

The third harmonic of a closed pipe has the same frequency as the first overtone of an open pipe 50 cm long. Find the length of the closed pipe. Model answer: The first overtone of an open pipe is its 2nd harmonic, $f = 2\times\dfrac{v}{2L_o} = \dfrac{v}{L_o}$. The third harmonic of a closed pipe is $f = \dfrac{3v}{4L_c}$. Equating the two,

A closed pipe 20 cm long has an internal radius of 2.0 cm. Taking $v = 340\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, find its fundamental frequency with and without the end correction. Model answer: Without correction, $f_1 = v/4L = 340/(4\times0.20) = 425\ \text{Hz}$. With correction, $e = 0.6\times0.020 = 0.012\ \text{m}$, so

A train travelling at $30\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in still air sounds a whistle of $262\ \text{Hz}$. A passenger on another train moving at $18\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in the opposite direction hears it. Find the frequency heard (i) Model answer: The passenger (observer) moves at $u_o = 18\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and the source at $u_s = 30\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. (i) Approaching:

A car horn of $400\ \text{Hz}$ is heard by a stationary listener with a frequency difference of $60\ \text{Hz}$ between approach and recession. Find the speed of the car ($v = 340\ \text{m s}^{-1}$). Model answer: For a source moving at speed $u$ past a stationary listener, the frequency on approach is $f_1 = \dfrac{fv}{v-u}$ and on recession $f_2 = \dfrac{fv}{v+u}$.

A train moving at $10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ towards a cliff sounds a horn of $600\ \text{Hz}$. Find the frequency of the echo heard by the driver [3] and explain why it is higher than $600\ \text{Hz}$. Model answer: The cliff first acts as a stationary observer receiving $f_1$ from the moving source, and then as a stationary source emitting $f_1$ to the moving driver:

Define intensity level in decibels. The intensity of a sound is $1.0\times10^{-5}\ \text{W m}^{-2}$; find its level ($I_0 = 10^{-12}\ \text{W m}^{-2}$). Model answer: (a) The intensity level is $\beta = 10\log_{10}(I/I_0)$ decibels, where $I_0 = 10^{-12}\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ is the threshold of hearing.

What is the Doppler effect? Derive the apparent frequency when a source moves towards a stationary observer and when an observer moves towards a stationary source. Model answer: (a) The Doppler effect is the apparent change in the frequency of a wave heard by an observer when there is relative motion between the source and the observer.

Explain the characteristics of sound. Derive the relation between displacement amplitude and pressure amplitude, $p_{max} = Bks_{max}$. Model answer: (a) See short answer 5: intensity (objective), loudness (subjective, depends on intensity and frequency), pitch (frequency) and quality (harmonic content).

Show that the pressure amplitude of a sound wave is $P_0 = \rho v\omega a$ and explain why the pressure wave leads the displacement wave by a quarter of a wavelength. Model answer: With $y = a\sin(\omega t-kx)$, $\Delta P = -B\,\partial y/\partial x = Bak\cos(\omega t-kx)$, so $P_0 = Bak$. Using $B=\rho v^{2}$ and $k=\omega/v$ gives $P_0 = \rho v\omega a$. The cosine leads the sine by $\pi/2$, which in space is a quarter wavelength.

The intensity level of a sound is 70 dB. Find its intensity, and the new intensity level if the intensity is increased 100 times. Model answer: $\beta = 10\log_{10}(I/I_0) = 70$ gives $I/I_0 = 10^{7}$, so $I = 10^{7}\times10^{-12} = 1.0\times10^{-5}\ \text{W m}^{-2}$. Multiplying the intensity by $100 = 10^{2}$ adds $10\log_{10}10^{2} = 20\ \text{dB}$, giving $\beta' = 90\ \text{dB}$.

State Huygens' principle. Use it to show how a plane wavefront passing through a small aperture becomes spherical. Model answer: (a) Huygens' principle: every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets, which spread out in all directions with the speed of the wave; the new wavefront after a time $t$ is the forward envelope (common tangent surface) of these wavelets.

Prove Snell's law using Huygens' construction. Light of wavelength $600\ \text{nm}$ in air passes into glass of refractive index $1.5$; find its speed, wavelength and frequency in glass. Model answer: (a) A plane wavefront $AB$ is incident on the boundary between medium 1 (speed $v_1$) and medium 2 ($v_2$), at angle of incidence $i$. While the wavelet from $B$ reaches the boundary at $C$ in time $t$ ($BC = v_1t$), the wavelet from $A$ travels $AD = v_2t$ in medium 2. The refracted wavefront is $CD$, making angle $r$

Name two phenomena explained by the wave theory and one that is not. What did Foucault's experiment settle? Model answer: (a) Explained by the wave theory: reflection and refraction (Huygens' construction), interference and diffraction (superposition, bending) and polarization (transverse waves). Not explained: the photoelectric effect, which needs energy in quanta (photons).

Define refractive index in terms of the speeds of light. A ray goes from water ($n = 1.33$) into glass ($n = 1.50$); find the ratio of the speeds and of the wavelengths. Model answer: (a) The refractive index of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in the medium: $n = c/v$.

Explain, using Huygens' principle, why light bends towards the normal on entering a denser medium. Derive the critical angle in terms of the speeds of light in the two media and find it for glass–air ($n = 1.5$). Model answer: (a) On entering a denser medium the end of the wavefront that arrives first slows down, while the other end is still moving at the higher speed. The wavefront therefore swings round, so its normal (the ray) turns towards the normal to the surface: $r<i$.

Define a wavefront and state Huygens' principle. Using it, show how a plane wavefront and a spherical wavefront advance. Model answer: Outline: wavefront = locus of points in the same phase; each point emits secondary wavelets of radius $vt$; new wavefront = forward envelope. A plane wavefront gives a plane envelope, a spherical one a larger sphere (Figure 1).

Explain why the frequency of light does not change on refraction while its wavelength does. Hence define optical path. Model answer: Outline: the vibrations in medium 2 are driven by those arriving from medium 1, so they repeat at the same rate — $f$ is fixed. Since $v = f\lambda$ and $v$ falls to $c/n$, the wavelength falls to $\lambda_0/n$. Optical path $= n \times$ geometrical path is the equivalent vacuum distance containing the same number of w

Define interference of light. What are coherent sources and how are they obtained in practice? Model answer: (a) Interference is the redistribution of energy produced when two or more coherent light waves overlap: bright fringes where they reinforce and dark fringes where they cancel.

Two waves of equal intensity $I$ superpose; find the resultant intensity for constructive and destructive interference. Write the general expression for the resultant intensity at phase difference $\phi$. Model answer: (a) Two waves of amplitude $a$ superpose with phase difference $\phi$: the resultant amplitude is $R = 2a\cos(\phi/2)$, so $I\propto R^{2} = 4a^{2}\cos^{2}(\phi/2)$, i.e. $I_R = 4I\cos^{2}(\phi/2)$. Constructive ($\phi = 0, 2\pi,\dots$): $I_{max} = 4I$. Destructive ($\phi = \pi, 3\pi,\dots$): $I_{min} = 0$.

What are coherent sources? Explain why two independent bulbs of the same colour cannot produce a steady interference pattern. Model answer: Outline: coherent = same frequency, constant phase difference. Model answer: Outline: $I = 4I_0\cos^2(\phi/2)$; the average of $\cos^2$ over a fringe is $\frac{1}{2}$, so the mean intensity is $2I_0$ — exactly the sum of the two beams. What is polarization of light? How can you tell a polaroid sunglass from an ordinary tinted one? Model answer: (a) Polarization is the restriction of the vibrations of the electric vector of a transverse wave to a single plane (plane of vibration), perpendicular to the direction of travel.

Why is Charles Babbage called the father of the computer? Model answer: Because his Analytical Engine (1834) was the first design for a general-purpose, programmable computer, and it had input (punched cards), a mill (processor), a store (memory) and output — the same units as modern computers.

Why is Ada Lovelace called the first programmer? Model answer: In 1843 she wrote notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine in which she set out step by step how the engine would calculate Bernoulli numbers. This is the first published computer program; she also foresaw that computers could work with symbols and music, not only numbers.

How did the Jacquard loom influence the development of computers? Model answer: The loom (1804) was controlled by punched cards: the pattern of holes decided the woven pattern. This showed that instructions could be stored on cards and changed without changing the machine; Babbage used the idea for the Analytical Engine and Hollerith for his census tabulator.

Write the full forms of EDVAC, UNIVAC, ABC and EDSAC. Model answer: EDVAC — Electronic Discrete Variable Automatic Computer; UNIVAC — Universal Automatic Computer; ABC — Atanasoff–Berry Computer; EDSAC — Electronic Delay Storage Automatic Calculator.

What is the stored-program concept? Why was it an improvement on ENIAC? Model answer: The stored-program concept (von Neumann, 1945) keeps the program's instructions in memory with the data. ENIAC had to be re-wired by hand to change its program, which took days; a stored-program computer just loads new instructions.

Write a short note on the IBM 1401 in Nepal. Model answer: The IBM 1401, a second-generation computer, was Nepal's first computer. It was brought on rent in 2028 BS (1971 AD), at Rs 1,25,000 a month, to process the census of 2028 BS at the Central Bureau of Statistics.

Describe the abacus, Napier's bones and the slide rule. Model answer: Abacus: the oldest calculating device (counting boards in Mesopotamia c. 2700 BC; the Chinese suanpan later). A frame of rods with beads; a beam divides heaven beads (worth 5) from earth beads (worth 1); beads moved to the beam are counted; used for addition and subtraction. Napier's bones: John Napier, Scotland, 1617.

Describe Babbage's Analytical Engine and explain why it is important. Model answer: Designed by Charles Babbage from 1834 as a general-purpose machine driven by steam. Its parts: input by punched cards (from the Jacquard loom) for numbers and operations; the mill, which did the arithmetic; the store, which held 1,000 numbers; and output by printer, curve plotter and bell. It could make decisions and r

Write any two features of first-generation computers. Model answer: Any two: they used vacuum tubes; they were huge, heavy and gave off great heat; they used a lot of electricity and failed often; they were programmed in machine language; their speed was measured in milliseconds.

What is a transistor? Write one advantage it had over the vacuum tube. Model answer: A transistor is a small electronic switch made of a semiconductor (invented at Bell Labs in 1947). Compared with a vacuum tube, it is far smaller, uses less electricity, gives off less heat and is more reliable.

What is an integrated circuit? Which generation used it first? Model answer: An integrated circuit (IC, or chip) is a small piece of silicon on which many transistors and other components are made together. ICs were first used in the third generation (about 1964–1975).

What is a microprocessor? Name the first microprocessor and its year. Model answer: A microprocessor is a single chip that contains the whole CPU of a computer. The first was the Intel 4004, made in 1971.

Explain fifth-generation computers: their technology, features and uses. Model answer: (1) Technology: artificial intelligence (AI) — computers that learn, reason and understand language — and parallel processing, in which many processors work on parts of a problem at the same time. (2) Features: they can understand natural (spoken and written) language, recognise faces and speech, and learn from data. (

What is meant by a generation of computer? Model answer: A generation of computer is a stage in the development of computers marked by a major new technology, especially a new main processing component. Each new generation was smaller, faster, cheaper, more reliable and more powerful than the one before.

Write any four features of first-generation computers. Model answer: Any four: vacuum tubes as the main component; magnetic drum memory; machine language; punched cards and paper tape for input; huge size; much heat and electricity; unreliable; slow (milliseconds); very expensive.

What is a transistor? Why was it better than a vacuum tube? Model answer: A transistor is a small semiconductor component that switches and amplifies electric current. It was better because it was much smaller, used less power, gave off little heat, was faster and lasted longer, so computers became smaller, cheaper and more reliable.

What is an integrated circuit? Who invented it? Model answer: An integrated circuit (chip) is a complete circuit of many transistors, resistors and capacitors made on one small piece of silicon. It was invented by Jack Kilby (1958), and independently by Robert Noyce (1959).

What is a microprocessor? Name the first microprocessor. Model answer: A microprocessor is a single chip that contains the whole CPU (control unit, ALU and registers). The first was the Intel 4004 (1971).
Write the full forms of IC, LSI, VLSI and ULSI. Model answer: IC — Integrated Circuit; LSI — Large Scale Integration; VLSI — Very Large Scale Integration; ULSI — Ultra Large Scale Integration.

What is artificial intelligence? Give two examples of its use. Model answer: AI is the ability of a computer program to do tasks that need human intelligence, such as understanding language, recognising faces, learning and deciding. Examples: voice assistants, face unlock, Google Translate, AI chatbots, self-driving cars (any two).

What is parallel processing? Give one example. Model answer: Parallel processing divides a big task into parts that several processors work on at the same time, so it finishes faster. Example: a supercomputer running a weather forecast on thousands of processors, or the eight cores of a phone processor.

A job takes 48 hours on one processor. Ideally, how long will it take on 6 processors? Why is the real time longer? Model answer: Ideal time = 48 ÷ 6 = 8 hours. It is longer in practice because the processors must share out the work, wait for each other and combine results, and some steps cannot be split.

Describe the features of second-generation computers with examples. Model answer: Period about 1958–1964. Main component: transistors (invented at Bell Labs in 1947) instead of vacuum tubes. Magnetic core memory; magnetic tape and disks for storage. Assembly language and the first high-level languages, FORTRAN and COBOL. Smaller, faster (microseconds), cheaper and more reliable than the first genera

What is the fifth generation of computers? Describe its features. Model answer: The fifth generation is the present and future stage in which computers use artificial intelligence to learn, reason and understand natural language (1 mark). Features: AI that learns from data and recognises speech, faces and writing; natural-language input in ordinary words; parallel processing on many processors; UL

The Intel 4004 (1971) had 2,300 transistors. Assuming the number doubles every two years, find the expected number in 1991. What is this rule called? Model answer: From 1971 to 1991 is 20 years = 20 ÷ 2 = 10 doublings. Expected number = 2,300 × $2^{10}$ = 2,300 × 1,024 = 2,355,200 (about 2.4 million). The rule is Moore's law. (The real Intel 486 of 1989 had about 1.2 million transistors, so the rule is a good rough guide.)

Write two uses of mainframe computers. Model answer: Mainframes serve thousands of users at the same time, so they are used by banks for customer accounts and by airlines and railways for ticket booking (also by governments for census and tax records).

Differentiate between a desktop and a laptop computer. Model answer: A desktop is designed to stay on a desk, with a separate monitor, keyboard and system unit, and is cheaper and easier to upgrade. A laptop has the screen, keyboard and battery in one portable unit, so it can be carried and used without mains power.

What are special-purpose computers? Give two examples. Model answer: Special-purpose computers are made to do only one particular task; when built into a machine they are called embedded systems. Examples: the computer in a washing machine, a traffic-light controller, an ATM, a digital camera.

Classify computers on the basis of size and explain each type briefly. Model answer: Supercomputer: the fastest and most expensive; used for weather and research. Mainframe: large, very powerful, used by thousands of users at once in banks and airlines. Minicomputer: medium-sized and multi-user, used by smaller organisations; today's servers do this job. Microcomputer: a computer built around a micropr

Which type of computer would you choose for each, and why: Model answer: (a) A mainframe (or powerful servers), because thousands of branch users must reach the same accounts at once. (b) A supercomputer, because forecasting needs huge numbers of calculations very fast. (c) A microcomputer — a desktop or laptop — which is cheap and enough for one user. (d) A workstation, a powerful microcom

Differentiate between analog and digital computers in two points. Model answer: An analog computer works on continuous data and measures; a digital computer works on discrete data (0 and 1) and counts. Analog results are approximate; digital results are exact. (Also: analog has little memory, digital has large memory.)

What is a hybrid computer? Give two examples. Model answer: A hybrid computer combines analog and digital features: it measures continuous quantities and then processes and displays them digitally. Examples: ECG machine, ICU patient monitor, petrol-pump dispenser.

What is a mainframe computer? Where is it used? Model answer: A mainframe is a large, powerful, very reliable computer that serves hundreds or thousands of users at the same time. It is used by banks, insurance companies, airlines, railways and large government offices.

What is a microcomputer? Why is it so popular? Model answer: A microcomputer is a small, low-cost computer with a single microprocessor as its CPU, used by one person at a time (a PC). It is popular because it is cheap, small, easy to use and runs millions of programs for study, work and entertainment.

Differentiate between a laptop and a desktop computer. Model answer: A desktop stays on a desk, has a separate system unit and needs mains power; a laptop is portable, has everything in one folding case and runs on a battery. A desktop gives more power for the money and is easier to upgrade; a laptop can be used anywhere.

What is a workstation? Who uses it? Model answer: A workstation is a powerful single-user microcomputer with a fast multi-core processor, large RAM and a professional graphics card. It is used by engineers, architects, animators, video editors and scientists.

What is an embedded system? Give two examples. Model answer: An embedded system is a special-purpose computer built into another machine to control it. Examples: the controller of a washing machine or microwave oven, an ATM, a car's airbag computer, a traffic-light controller.

A supercomputer does $2 \times 10^{18}$ calculations per second and a laptop $10^{12}$. How many seconds would the laptop take to do the supercomputer's work of one second? Model answer: Time = $2 \times 10^{18} \div 10^{12} = 2 \times 10^{6}$ s = 2,000,000 seconds (about 23 days).

What is a hybrid computer? Explain with three examples how it combines analog and digital features. Model answer: A hybrid computer combines an analog part that measures continuous quantities with a digital part that calculates, stores and displays (1 mark). ECG machine: measures the heart's electrical signal (analog) and displays and prints it as a trace with values (digital). ICU monitor: measures heart rate, blood pressure and

Describe any four types of microcomputer. Model answer: Any four. Desktop: stays on a desk; separate system unit, monitor, keyboard and mouse; powerful for its price; school labs and offices. Laptop: portable, all parts in one folding case with a battery; study and office work anywhere. Tablet: flat, light, touch screen; reading, videos, classes. Smartphone: a phone that ru

(b) A hybrid computer (ICU monitor): it measures heart rate, pressure and oxygen continuously and shows exact values and alarms. What is a device driver? Why is it needed? Model answer: A device driver is a small program that lets the operating system communicate with one particular hardware device, such as a printer, webcam or graphics card. Without the right driver the device does not work, or works badly.

What are utility programs? Give two examples. Model answer: Utility programs are system programs that maintain, protect and tidy the computer. Examples: antivirus, backup software, file compression (WinRAR, 7-Zip), Disk Cleanup.

Differentiate between packaged and tailor-made software. Model answer: Packaged software is ready-made for many users and sold or given in the market, such as MS Office or VLC. Tailor-made (customised) software is built for the needs of one organisation, such as a school's result system or a bank's account system.

Differentiate between freeware and shareware. Model answer: Freeware can be used free of cost for ever, but its source code is not given (for example Google Chrome, Adobe Acrobat Reader). Shareware can be tried free for a limited time or with limited features, after which the user must pay (for example WinRAR's trial).

Explain the four kinds of system software. Model answer: Operating system: manages all hardware and software and provides the user interface (Windows, Linux). Device drivers: let the OS control each device. Utility programs: maintain and protect the computer (antivirus, backup, compression). Language processors: translate programs into machine code — assembler, compiler and

Explain proprietary and open-source software with examples. Why is software piracy wrong? Model answer: Proprietary software is owned by a company; users buy a licence to use it, and the source code is secret and may not be changed or shared (MS Windows, MS Office, Adobe Photoshop). Open-source software is free to use, and its source code is open for anyone to study, change and share (Linux, LibreOffice, GIMP, Firefox).

What is software? Write two reasons why it is important. Model answer: Software is a set of programs that tells the computer's hardware what to do. It is important because hardware cannot work without it, and because it makes the computer versatile — the same machine does many tasks by running different software. (Also: lets people use the computer easily; solves problems in every field.)

Differentiate between system software and application software. Model answer: System software controls and manages the hardware and runs whenever the computer is on (e.g. Windows, drivers). Application software helps the user do a particular task and runs only when opened (e.g. MS Word, Chrome).

What is a utility program? Name any three. Model answer: A utility program is system software that maintains, protects or improves the computer and its data. Examples: antivirus (Microsoft Defender), file compression (7-Zip), disk cleanup, backup, Task Manager.

Differentiate between a compiler and an interpreter in two points. Model answer: A compiler translates the whole program at once and makes a separate machine-code file; an interpreter translates and runs one line at a time and makes no file. A compiler lists all errors after translating; an interpreter stops at the first error. (E.g. C uses a compiler; Python an interpreter.)

Differentiate between packaged and tailor-made software, with one example of each. Model answer: Packaged software is ready-made for many users with common needs and is cheaper, e.g. Microsoft Excel. Tailor-made software is written for one organization's own needs and is costlier, e.g. a school's own result-processing system.

What is open-source software? Give two examples. Model answer: Open-source software is software whose source code is open for anyone to use, read, change and share under its licence; it is usually free. Examples: Linux, LibreOffice, Firefox, VLC, Python (any two).

Why should software be updated regularly? Give two reasons. Model answer: Updates fix bugs (mistakes) in programs and close security holes that viruses and hackers use; they also add new features and keep the software working with new hardware and files.

What is system software? Explain its four types with examples. Model answer: System software is the group of programs that controls and manages the hardware and provides a base for application software (1 mark). Operating system: manages hardware, memory, files and programs and gives the user an interface — Windows 11, Linux, Android. Device drivers: let the OS control one device — a printer or

Model answer: Proprietary: owned by a company, code secret, must buy a licence, cannot copy or change — Microsoft Windows, MS Office. Freeware: free of cost to use, but code closed and cannot be changed — Google Chrome, Zoom. Differentiate between CUI and GUI operating systems. Model answer: In a CUI (character user interface) the user types commands, as in MS-DOS or the Linux terminal; it needs commands to be remembered. In a GUI (graphical user interface) the user clicks windows, icons, menus and buttons with a mouse or a finger, as in Windows or Android; it is easy for beginners.

What is a file extension? Write two examples with the type of file. Model answer: A file extension is the part of a file name after the dot that shows the type of file. Examples:.docx — a Word document;.jpg — a photograph;.mp3 — a sound file;.exe — a program (any two).

Differentiate between copying and moving a file, with the shortcut keys. Model answer: Copying makes a duplicate in the new place and leaves the original where it was (Ctrl + C, then Ctrl + V). Moving takes the file to the new place and removes it from the old one (Ctrl + X, then Ctrl + V).

What is the Recycle Bin? How can a file be restored from it? Model answer: The Recycle Bin is a folder where Windows keeps files deleted from the hard disk, so that they can be recovered. To restore a file, open the Recycle Bin, select the file and click Restore; it returns to its old folder. (Files deleted with Shift + Delete, or from a pen drive, skip the Recycle Bin.)

Explain single-user and multi-user, and desktop and mobile operating systems, with examples. Model answer: A single-user OS lets one person use the computer at a time (Windows 11 Home). A multi-user OS lets many users work on it at the same time, usually over a network (Linux servers, UNIX). A desktop OS runs on desktops and laptops (Windows, macOS, Linux). A mobile OS runs on smartphones and tablets and is designed for tou

Define operating system. Name two examples. Model answer: An operating system is system software that controls and manages all the hardware and software of a computer and provides an interface between the user and the computer. Examples: Windows 11, Linux, macOS, Android, iOS (any two).

Write any four functions of an operating system. Model answer: Any four: process management (runs programs, multitasking); memory management; file management; device management through drivers; security and user accounts; providing the user interface; booting.

Differentiate between CUI and GUI. Model answer: In a CUI the user types commands and sees only text, e.g. MS-DOS; in a GUI the user clicks windows, icons and menus, e.g. Windows. A CUI needs remembered commands and little memory; a GUI is easy to learn but needs more memory and processing power.

Differentiate between single-user and multi-user operating systems. Model answer: A single-user OS lets one user work at a time, e.g. Windows 11 Home on a PC. A multi-user OS lets many users work on one computer at the same time through terminals or a network, keeping their work separate, e.g. Linux or UNIX servers.

What is a mobile operating system? Name two. Model answer: A mobile operating system runs on smartphones and tablets; it is designed for touch, small screens and battery saving, and uses the camera, GPS and mobile network. Examples: Android and iOS.

What is a dialog box? Name any three of its controls. Model answer: A dialog box is a small window in which a program asks the user for information or a choice before carrying out a command. Controls (any three): tabs, text box, drop-down list, check box, option button, spin box, command buttons (OK, Cancel, Apply).

Differentiate between a file and a folder. Model answer: A file is a named collection of related data, such as a document or photo, e.g. essay.docx. A folder is a named container that holds files and other folders to keep them organized, e.g. Documents.

Write the difference between copying and moving a file. Model answer: Copying (Ctrl + C, Ctrl + V) keeps the original and makes a duplicate in the new place; moving (Ctrl + X, Ctrl + V) removes the file from the old place and puts it only in the new place.

What is the Recycle Bin? How can a deleted file be restored? Model answer: The Recycle Bin is a special folder that keeps files deleted from the computer's own drives so that they can be restored. To restore: open the Recycle Bin, select the file and click Restore the selected items (or right-click → Restore); it returns to its original folder.

What is an operating system? Explain any three functions. Model answer: An operating system is system software that manages the hardware and software and provides the user interface (1 mark). Write any four features of a word processor and name two word processors. Model answer: Any four: typing and editing text; formatting text and paragraphs; spelling and grammar checking; inserting tables, pictures and shapes; headers, footers and page numbers; mail merge; saving and printing. Word processors: Microsoft Word, LibreOffice Writer, Google Docs (any two).

Differentiate between Save and Save As. Model answer: Save (Ctrl + S) stores the document under its present name and place; the first time, it asks for a name. Save As (F12 in Word) saves a copy under a new name, in a new place or in another format, keeping the old file as it was.

Differentiate between cut and copy. Write their shortcut keys. Model answer: Cut (Ctrl + X) removes the selected text and keeps it on the clipboard to be pasted elsewhere; copy (Ctrl + C) keeps the text in its place and puts a copy on the clipboard. Both are pasted with Ctrl + V.

What is Find and Replace? Write its shortcut keys. Model answer: Find (Ctrl + F) searches the document for a word or phrase. Replace (Ctrl + H) finds a word and changes it to another, one at a time or all at once with Replace All — for example changing every "Kathmandu" to "Lalitpur".

Explain font formatting, paragraph formatting, bullets and numbering, and page layout. Model answer: Font formatting: changing the font type, size, colour and style (bold, italic, underline) of characters. Paragraph formatting: alignment (left, centre, right, justify), line spacing, indentation and space before and after. Bullets and numbering: making lists that start with symbols or numbers. What are header, footer and page numbers? How can a table and a picture be inserted into a document? Model answer: A header is text printed at the top of every page and a footer at the bottom (such as the school name or a date); page numbers number the pages automatically (Insert → Header, Footer, Page Number). What is a word processor? Name two examples. Model answer: A word processor is application software used to create, edit, format, save and print text documents. Examples: Microsoft Word, LibreOffice Writer, Google Docs (any two).

Write any four features of a word processor. Model answer: Any four: word wrap; editing with cut, copy, paste and undo; find and replace; spelling and grammar check; formatting of fonts, paragraphs and pages; tables, pictures and shapes; headers, footers and page numbers; mail merge; saving as PDF; templates.

Differentiate between Cut and Copy. Model answer: Cut (Ctrl + X) removes the selected text and keeps it on the clipboard, so pasting moves it. Copy (Ctrl + C) leaves the text where it is and puts a copy on the clipboard, so pasting duplicates it.

Write the steps to find the word "Kathmandu" and replace it with "Lalitpur" everywhere in a document. Model answer: Press Ctrl + H (Home → Editing → Replace). Type Kathmandu in Find what and Lalitpur in Replace with; under More, tick Find whole words only if needed; click Replace All, then OK.

Write the steps to insert page numbers at the bottom of every page in Word. Model answer: Insert tab → Page Number → Bottom of Page → choose a style such as Plain Number 2; then click Close Header and Footer.

Write the steps to insert a table of 4 columns and 6 rows. Model answer: Place the cursor; Insert → Table → Insert Table…; type 4 in Number of columns and 6 in Number of rows; click OK. (In Writer: Table → Insert Table.)

What is meant by text wrapping? Name two wrapping options. Model answer: Text wrapping decides how the text of the document flows around a picture or shape. Options (any two): In Line with Text, Square, Tight, Top and Bottom, Behind Text, In Front of Text.
Write the shortcut keys for: bold, centre alignment, paste and print. Model answer: Bold: Ctrl + B; centre: Ctrl + E; paste: Ctrl + V; print: Ctrl + P.

Define workbook, worksheet, cell and range, with an example of a cell address and a range. A cell is the box where a row and a column meet; its address is column letter plus row number, such as B3. A range is a block of cells, such as A1:D5 (from A1 to D5).

A cell address is its column letter and row number, e.g. C2. A range is a rectangular block of cells written first:last, e.g. B2:E6.

Differentiate between a workbook and a worksheet. Model answer: A workbook is the whole spreadsheet file (e.g. Marks.xlsx); a worksheet is one grid of rows and columns inside it, chosen by a sheet tab. One workbook can hold many worksheets.

Differentiate between a formula and a function, with an example of each. Model answer: A formula is any calculation the user writes, beginning with =, e.g. =B2+C2+D2. A function is a built-in, named formula, e.g. =SUM(B2:D2). Functions can be used inside formulas.

What is AutoFill? Write what appears when "Monday" is filled down three cells. Model answer: AutoFill copies cell contents or continues a series when the fill handle is dragged. Filling "Monday" down three cells gives Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday.

Differentiate between relative and absolute cell references. Model answer: A relative reference (B2) changes when the formula is copied, by the number of rows and columns moved. An absolute reference ($B$2) stays fixed on the same cell when copied, e.g. a VAT rate in one cell.

Differentiate between sorting and filtering. Model answer: Sorting rearranges all the rows in ascending or descending order of a column; filtering shows only the rows that meet a condition and hides the others without changing their order.
